01 | Prostate Cancer | The most common solid neoplasm in Europe and the second most common cause of cancer death in men. Diagnosis is based on clinical findings, PSA, imaging, biopsy and Gleason grading; treatment depends on stage. | URO-ONCOLOGY · SECTION 01

Prostate Cancer · 1/8 | Incidence & Risk Factors | Factors determining the risk of clinical PCa are not well known; a few have been identified | Incidence | In Europe, PCa is the most common solid neoplasm — incidence 214 cases per 1000 | Currently the second most common cause of cancer death in men | Three Well-Established Risk Factors | Increasing age | — the single most important demographic factor | Ethnic origin | — e.g., Japanese men have a low incidence of PCa | Heredity | — family history is a strong determinant | Heredity — Quantified Risk | One first-line relative with PCa → risk is at least doubled | Two or more first-line relatives affected → risk increases 5–11-fold | Clinical Note | Most early-stage cancers are asymptomatic; risk factors determine who needs screening with PSA and digital rectal examination. Heredity remains the strongest patient-level signal after age and ethnicity.

Prostate Cancer · 2/8 | Diagnosis — Clinical Findings & PSA | Symptoms, signs and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) | A. Symptoms | Most patients with early-stage PCa are asymptomatic | Presence of symptoms often suggests locally advanced or metastatic disease | Obstructive or irritative voiding complaints result from local growth of the tumour into the urethra or bladder neck, or from its direct extension | B. Signs | A physical examination, including a digital rectal examination (DRE), is needed. | Induration, if detected, must alert the physician to the possibility of cancer and the need for further evaluation. | Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) | Glycoprotein acting as a serine protease | Produced by benign and malignant prostate tissues | Normal PSA values: ≤ 2.5 – 4 ng/mL (according to age) | PSA Derivatives | Free/total PSA ratio | — ratio | PSA density | — PSA ÷ prostate volume = 0.15; a value above 0.15 means high susceptibility for cancer

Prostate Cancer · 3/8 | Diagnostic Modalities & Staging Tools | Imaging, biopsy and staging evaluation | Core Diagnostic Steps | Transrectal ultrasonography (TRUS) | Prostate biopsy guided by TRUS | Diagnostic transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) | Local Staging (T-Staging) | Based on magnetic resonance (MR) imaging | Number and sites of positive prostate biopsies, tumour grade and serum PSA level provide further information | Dynamic contrast-enhanced MR (DCE-MRI) helpful in equivocal cases | Metastasis Staging (M-Staging) | Small metastases ( | Skeletal metastasis best assessed by bone scan | In equivocal cases: PET/CT or whole-body MRI are an option | PSA is the key biochemical marker; TRUS-guided biopsy confirms histology; MR imaging stages the primary tumour; bone scan and PLND address skeletal and nodal spread respectively.

Prostate Cancer · 4/8 | Gleason Score — Histological Grading | The current standard for grading adenocarcinoma of the prostate | Principles | Over 95% of prostate cancers are adenocarcinomas | Gleason score is the current standard for grading adenocarcinoma of the prostate | Relies on the low-power appearance of the glandular architecture under the microscope | Grades adenocarcinoma into five grades (patterns 1–5) | Score = sum of the two most common patterns of tumour growth found | Score ranges 2–10: 2 = least aggressive, 10 = most aggressive | Patterns 1–5 — Glandular Architecture | Grade 1 | well-formed, closely packed glands | Grade 2 | separated, still well-formed glands | Grade 3 | infiltrative glands, variable size | Grade 4 | fused, poorly formed glands | Grade 5 | no glandular differentiation, sheets of cells

Prostate Cancer · 5/8 | Hormonal Therapy — The Androgen Axis | Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) and the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis | A | Hypothalamus | Secretes luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) | B | Anterior Pituitary | LHRH stimulates release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) | C | Leydig Cells of the Testes | LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone | D | Prostate Cell | Testosterone → 5-α-dihydrotestosterone (DHT) by 5-α-reductase; DHT is ~10× more powerful as an androgenic stimulant | Why Deprivation Works | If prostate cells are deprived of androgenic stimulation, they undergo apoptosis (programmed cell death) | Any treatment that ultimately suppresses androgen activity is androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) | Two Routes of Androgen Deprivation | Suppress secretion of testicular androgens | — surgical or medical castration | Inhibit action of circulating androgens | — at the receptor in prostate cells, using competing compounds known as anti-androgens | Complete Androgen Blockade (CAB) | The two methods (surgical or medical castration + anti-androgens) can be combined to achieve complete (or maximal / total) androgen blockade (CAB).

Prostate Cancer · 6/8 | Methods of Androgen Deprivation | Sites of action of hormonal therapy: LHRH agonist/antagonist · orchiectomy · anti-androgens | Bilateral Orchiectomy | Surgical castration — removes testicular androgen production | LHRH Agonists | Long-acting agonists: busereline, gosereline, leuproreline, triptoreline | Medical castration via pituitary LHRH-receptor stimulation | LHRH Antagonists | In contrast to agonists: bind immediately and competitively to LHRH receptors in the pituitary gland | Anti-Androgens | Compete with testosterone and DHT at the receptor level in the prostate cell nucleus | Thus promoting apoptosis and inhibiting PCa growth | Estrogens — Mechanisms of Action | Down-regulation of LHRH secretion | Androgen inactivation | Direct suppression of Leydig cell function | Direct cytotoxicity to the prostate epithelium (in-vitro evidence only) | Complete Androgen Blockade (CAB) | Combination of castration (surgical or medical) with anti-androgens | Commonly known as complete / maximal / total androgen blockade

Prostate Cancer · 7/8 | Treatment by Stage — Table 1 (Stage T1) | Treatment options depend on Gleason score, life expectancy and tumour differentiation | Stage | Treatment | Comment | T1 | Watchful waiting | Standard treatment for Gleason score | Active surveillance | 10-year life expectancy; re-staging with TRUS and biopsy is recommended | Radical prostatectomy | 7 adenocarcinomas | Radiotherapy | Optional in younger patients with a long life expectancy, in particular in poorly differentiated tumours; higher complication risks after TURP, especially with interstitial radiation | Hormonal | Not an option | Combination | Not an option

Prostate Cancer · 8/8 | Treatment by Stage — Table 2 (Stage T2) | Curative options for clinically localized disease | Stage | Treatment | Comment | T2 | Radical prostatectomy | 10 years | Radiotherapy | 10 years who accept treatment-related complications | Brachytherapy | Low-dose rate brachytherapy can be considered for low-risk PCa patients with a prostate volume | Hormonal | Symptomatic patients who need palliation of symptoms, unfit for curative treatment | Combination | For high-risk patients | 10 years; hormonal therapy is reserved for palliation.

02 | Bladder Cancer | A disease driven by environmental carcinogens and chronic irritation. From urothelial carcinoma and its grades to patterns of spread, TNM staging and the surgical/endoscopic treatment of non-muscle and muscle-invasive disease. | URO-ONCOLOGY · SECTION 02

Bladder Cancer · 1/9 | Epidemiology & Carcinogenesis | Chemical carcinogens and alterations in DNA | Molecular Basis | Chemical carcinogens | Alterations in DNA often lead to induction of oncogenes (p21 ras oncogene) or reversal of tumour suppressor genes (p53), resulting in a malignantly transformed cell | Key Epidemiology | More than 2.5× more common in men than in women | In men: fourth most common cancer after prostate, lung and colorectal cancers | Mortality rate: 22% of patients with bladder cancer per year | Inducing Agents | Viruses | Chemical carcinogens — aniline dyes | Cigarette smoking — nitrosamines, 2-naphthylamine, 4-aminobiphenyl, increased urinary tryptophan metabolites | Coffee drinking | Ingestion of analgesics (containing phenacetin) or artificial sweeteners | Bacterial, parasitic, fungal and viral infections | Harboring of bladder calculi | Receiving genotoxic chemotherapeutic agents

Bladder Cancer · 2/9 | Pathology — Urothelial Carcinoma & Tumour Grading | Carcinoma in Situ (CIS) | May appear as a velvety patch of erythematous mucosa, although quite often it is endoscopically invisible | Histologically: poorly differentiated transitional cell carcinoma confined to the urothelium | Transitional Cell Carcinoma (TCC) | Urothelial (transitional cell) cancers differ from normal urothelium by an increased number of epithelial cell layers with papillary folding of the mucosa | Old Grading System (WHO 1974) | Grade 1 — well differentiated | — thin fibrovascular stalk; thickened urothelium with more than seven cell layers; only slight anaplasia and pleomorphism | Grade 2 — moderately differentiated | — wider fibrovascular core; greater disturbance of base-to-surface maturation; loss of cell polarity; higher nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, more nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli | Grade 3 — poorly differentiated | — cells do not differentiate from basement membrane to surface; marked nuclear pleomorphism; high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio; mitotic figures may be frequent | New Grading System (WHO 2004) | Urothelial papilloma | Papillary urothelial neoplasm of low malignant potential (PUNLMP) | Low grade urothelial carcinoma | High grade urothelial carcinoma

Bladder Cancer · 3/9 | Pathology — Squamous Cell Carcinoma & Adenocarcinoma | Geographic variability and chronic irritation | Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) | Prevalence varies worldwide: 1% of bladder cancers in England, 3–7% in the United States, 40–75% in Egypt | About 80% of SCCs in Egypt are associated with chronic infection with S. haematobium | Patients are on average 10–20 years younger than patients with TCC | Bilharzial cancers: exophytic, nodular, fungating lesions, usually well differentiated, with a relatively low incidence of lymph node and distant metastases | Whether the low metastasis rate is due to capillary and lymphatic fibrosis from chronic schistosomal infection or to the low histologic grade is not clear | Non-Bilharzial SCC & Adenocarcinoma | Non-bilharzial SCC: chronic irritation from urinary calculi, long-term indwelling catheters, chronic urinary infections, or bladder diverticula | As many as 80% of paraplegics with chronic infections and/or indwelling catheters have squamous changes in the bladder; about 5% develop squamous cell carcinoma | Adenocarcinomas account for less than 2% of primary bladder cancers | Adenocarcinoma — Three Origins | 1 — Primary vesical | 2 — Urachal | 3 — Metastatic

Bladder Cancer · 4/9 | Patterns of Spread | Direct extension, lymphatic, vascular and implantation spread | Direct Extension (Local Invasion) | En bloc spread (~60%) | — cancer cells invade in a broad front directly beneath the primary mucosal lesion | Tentacle-like invasion (~25%) | — finger-like infiltration into the wall | Lateral spread (~10%) | — tumour cells grow under normal-appearing mucosa | Implantation | Bladder cancer also spreads by implantation in abdominal wounds, denuded urothelium, resected prostatic fossa, or traumatized urethra. | 1 — Lymphatic Spread (pelvic nodes) | Lymphatic metastases occur earlier and independently of haematogenous metastases in some patients | Patients with limited nodal metastases may be cured with radical cystectomy and pelvic lymphadenectomy | Paravesical nodes | — 16% | Obturator nodes | — 74% | External iliac nodes | — 65% | Presacral nodes | — ~25% | Juxtaregional common iliac nodes | — ~20% | 2 — Vascular Spread | Liver | — 38% | Lung | — 36% | Bone | — 27% | Adrenal glands | — 21% | Intestine | — 13% | Bone metastases are considerably more common with bilharzial bladder cancer

Bladder Cancer · 5/9 | Natural History & Clinical Presentation | What the patient experiences and what the tumour does | Natural History | Roughly 55–60% of all newly diagnosed bladder cancers are well- or moderately differentiated, superficial (confined to urothelium or lamina propria) papillary transitional cell carcinomas | 40–45% of newly diagnosed bladder cancers are high-grade lesions — more than half are muscle invading or more extensive at the time of diagnosis | Other Signs & Symptoms | Flank pain from ureteral obstruction | Lower extremity edema | Pelvic mass | Very rarely: symptoms of advanced disease — weight loss, abdominal or bone pain | Most Common Presentation | Painless hematuria | — occurs in about 85% of patients | Bladder irritability + urinary frequency, urgency, dysuria | — second most common presentation; usually associated with diffuse carcinoma in situ or invasive bladder cancer | These symptoms almost never occur without (at least) microscopic hematuria | Hematuria is the hallmark: painless hematuria in ~85% of patients is the most common presenting symptom of bladder cancer.

Bladder Cancer · 6/9 | Diagnostic Workup | Cytology, imaging and endoscopic evaluation | Conventional Microscopic Cytology | Malignant urothelial cells observed in urinary sediment or bladder washings | Tumour cells have large nuclei with irregular, coarsely textured chromatin | Limitations: cells from well-differentiated tumours look cytologically normal and are more cohesive (not readily shed) | More sensitive in high-grade tumours or carcinoma in situ | May be falsely negative in 20% even with high-grade tumours | Excretory Urography (IVU) | Indicated in all patients with signs and symptoms suggestive of bladder cancer | Not a sensitive means of detecting bladder tumours, particularly small ones | Useful for examining the upper urinary tracts for associated urothelial tumours | Large tumours may appear as filling defects in the bladder on the cystogram phase | Ureteral obstruction by a bladder tumour usually signals muscle-invasive cancer | Cystoscopy & Biopsy | All patients suspected of having bladder cancer should have careful cystoscopy and bimanual examination | Abnormal areas should be biopsied; random or selected-site mucosal biopsy specimens may also be obtained | Retrograde pyelography if the upper tracts are not adequately visualized on the excretory urogram | Ideal resection: resect the bulk of the tumour, then the deep portion with underlying bladder muscle, sending each specimen separately for histology | Cross-Sectional Imaging | CT scan | — assesses extent of primary tumour, pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenopathy and visceral metastases; should be done before TUR to accurately assess depth of penetration | MRI scan | — not much more helpful than CT scanning | Ultrasonography | — visualizes intravesical growth; used for follow-up of upper urinary tract dilatation due to obstruction by the tumour

Bladder Cancer · 7/9 | Staging — AJCC/UICC TNM System (1997) | Tumour, node and metastasis classification | Primary Tumour (T) | Stage | Extent | Ta | Papillary epithelium-confined tumour | Tis | Flat in situ carcinoma | T1 | Invasion of the lamina propria | T2a / T2b | Muscle-invasive — superficial / deep muscle invasion | T3a / T3b | Perivesical fat — microscopic / macroscopic invasion | T4a | Invasion of pelvic viscera: prostatic stroma, rectum, uterus or vagina | T4b | Extension to pelvic sidewalls or abdominal wall | Lymph Nodes (N) & Metastasis (M) | Regional nodes = nodes of the true pelvis below the bifurcation of the common iliac arteries | Laterality does not affect the N classification | N1 | — single positive node ≤ 2 cm in diameter | N2 | 2 cm but | N3 | 5 cm in diameter | No particular stage exists for juxtaregional lymph nodes | M0 / M1 | — absence / presence of distant metastases | Nx / Mx | — nodal or distant status uncertain | Developed jointly by the International Union Against Cancer (UICC) and the AJCC; the 1997 system is termed Tumour-Node-Metastasis (TNM).

Bladder Cancer · 8/9 | Treatment — Non-Muscle & Muscle-Invasive Disease | Endoscopic control for superficial disease; radical surgery for invasive disease | Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer (NMIBC) | 1 — TURBT: tumour visualized via cystoscope, resected with a specialized endoscopic resectoscope; aim to resect the whole lesion with a sample from the underlying muscle layer to assess invasion; if complete resection impossible → representative biopsy including underlying muscle | 2 — Intravesical therapy: after complete resection, instillation of chemotherapy (mitomycin C) or immunotherapy (BCG) reduces the risk of tumour recurrence | 3 — Photodynamic diagnosis: instillation of photosensitizers (e.g., hexa-aminolaevulinic acid, HALA) enhances visualization of small bladder tumours; HALA instilled via a urethral catheter one hour before the procedure | 4 — Radical cystectomy: for high-grade NMIBC failing to respond to TURBT and intravesical therapy | 5 — Cystoscopic follow-up required to check for tumour recurrence | Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer (MIBC) | 1 — Radical cystectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy is the treatment of choice | 2 — Chemotherapy can be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) or after surgery (adjuvant) in cases of advanced tumours | 3 — Combined chemo-radiotherapy is an alternative to radical cystectomy in patients who are unfit for surgery, who refuse surgery, or who have fixed irresectable tumours | BCG = Bacillus Calmette-Guérin; TURBT = transurethral resection of bladder tumour.

03 | Urothelial Tumors of the Upper Urinary Tract | Neoplastic growths of the lining of the urinary tract from the calyces to the distal ureter — their pathology, patterns of spread, staging and the surgical gold standard of radical nephroureterectomy. | URO-ONCOLOGY · SECTION 03

Upper Urinary Tract · 1/5 | Introduction & Risk Factors | From the calyces to the distal ureter | Introduction | Any neoplastic growth involving the lining of the urinary tract from the calyces to the distal ureter | TCC most common in the bladder, then renal pelvis, least in the ureter (125 : 2.5 : 1) | 5–10% of upper urinary tract neoplasms; 2–4% bilateral | females | Typically presents with hematuria in 60–90% | 1/3 present with flank pain or acute renal colic; 15% discovered incidentally at radiologic examination | Risk of developing bladder TCC is 50% in patients with upper tract TCC; associated upper tract TCC in patients with bladder TCC is 5% | Risk Factors | Male gender and increasing age | Smoking | — most important risk factor; 2–3× (chemical carcinogens: aniline, benzidine, aromatic amine, azo dyes) | Exposure to chemotherapy such as cyclophosphamide | Heavy caffeine consumption | Chronic inflammation or infection | Occupational exposure in petroleum and plastic industries | Analgesic abuse | Balkan nephropathy | Hematuria is the dominant presentation; smoking is the single most important modifiable risk factor.

Upper Urinary Tract · 2/5 | Pathology | Benign lesions, abnormal urothelium and spread | Benign Lesions | 1 — Inverted papilloma: may be benign or have malignant potential | 2 — Fibroepithelial polyps and neurofibromas | Abnormal Urothelium | 1 — Metaplasia and dysplasia | 2 — Carcinoma in situ: whitish plaque or velvety red patch | 3 — TCC in more than 90% of upper tract tumours; may be sessile or papillary | 4 — SCC in 7% of cases; associated with chronic inflammation or analgesic abuse | 5 — Adenocarcinoma in 1% of cases | 6 — Sarcomas very rare | Spread — Four Routes | 1 — Direct invasion | — to the renal parenchyma or surrounding structures | 2 — Lymphatic invasion | — para-aortic, para-caval, iliac and pelvic lymph nodes | 3 — Vascular invasion | — liver, lung, bone | 4 — Epithelial spread | — by seeding or direct extension — e.g., recurrence of a ureteral stump left in situ after nephrectomy | 90% of upper tract tumours; SCC relates to chronic inflammation or analgesic abuse.

Upper Urinary Tract · 3/5 | Diagnosis | Clinical presentation, laboratory and imaging investigations | Clinical Presentation | Hematuria (gross or microscopic) | — the most common presenting symptom | Flank pain | — typically dull — gradual obstruction and hydronephrotic distention; can be acute, mimicking renal colic due to passage of clots | Asymptomatic | — discovered incidentally on radiologic evaluation | Advanced disease | — flank or abdominal pain, weight loss, anorexia, or bone pain | Laboratory | Urine analysis and culture | Urine cytology: directly related to tumour grade | Imaging | U/S | — detects hydronephrosis or pelvic mass | IVU | — suggestive findings: a) radiolucent filling defect; b) obstruction of part of the tract; c) non-visualization of the collecting system | CT scanning | — higher accuracy: parenchymal lesion, extent of invasion, associated lesions, enlarged lymph nodes and metastasis | Renal scan | — determines function of the diseased and the contralateral kidney | Endoscopy | Cystoscopy — to exclude coexistent bladder lesions | Ureteroscopy evaluation and biopsy — biopsy of suspected areas

Upper Urinary Tract · 4/5 | Staging — T Classification | Primary tumour staging for renal pelvis and ureter | T Stage Definitions | Stage | Definition | TX | Primary tumour cannot be assessed | T0 | No evidence of primary tumour | Ta | Non-invasive papillary carcinoma | Tis | Carcinoma in situ | T1 | Tumour invades subepithelial connective tissue | T2 | Tumour invades muscularis | T3 | Renal pelvis: beyond muscularis into peripelvic fat or renal parenchyma — Ureter: beyond muscularis into periureteric fat | T4 | Tumour invades adjacent organs or through the kidney into perinephric fat | Key Points | Ta/Tis/T1: non-invasive or superficially invasive — amenable to endoscopic or topical therapy | T2 and beyond: invasion of the muscularis — radical surgery is the standard | T3 differs by site: peripelvic fat / renal parenchyma (pelvis) vs periureteric fat (ureter) | T4: adjacent organs or perinephric fat involvement | The T stage, together with grade, multifocality and renal function, drives the choice between radical nephroureterectomy and endoscopic management.

Upper Urinary Tract · 5/5 | Treatment | Radical surgery, endoscopic management and topical/advanced therapy | Radical Nephroureterectomy + Bladder Cuff Excision (open or laparoscopy) | The gold standard for treatment of upper tract tumours in: | 1 — Large, high-grade invasive tumour | 2 — Large, multifocal, or rapidly recurring non-invasive tumour of the renal pelvis or proximal ureter | The kidney and the entire ureter including the orifice should be removed | Rationale: biologic behaviour characterized by multifocality, high incidence of ipsilateral recurrence after partial resection, and low incidence of contralateral disease | Endoscopic Resection or Fulguration (retrograde or antegrade) | Lesion first sampled, then underlying tissue ablated by electrocautery or laser | Indications: 1 — solitary kidney; 2 — bilateral disease; 3 — renal dysfunction; 4 — intercurrent illness precluding abdominal procedure; 5 — selected cases with small, low-grade lesions and a normal contralateral kidney | Disadvantages: recurrence and progression to invasive disease | Topical & Systemic Therapy | Topical immunotherapy (BCG) and chemotherapy (mitomycin C) | — reduce recurrence in non-invasive upper tract urothelial TCC | Instillation methods | — through a percutaneous tube; retrograde reflux from the bladder with a double J stent; instillation through a retrograde catheter | Advanced cases — chemotherapy | — MVAC (methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin, cisplatin) or combination of gemcitabine and taxanes

04 | Renal Tumors | From frequently incidental benign lesions (cysts, oncocytomas, angiomyolipomas) to renal cell carcinoma — pathology, the 2017 TNM staging and treatment of localized and metastatic disease. | URO-ONCOLOGY · SECTION 04

Renal Tumors · 1/4 | Benign Renal Tumors | Cysts, oncocytomas, angiomyolipomas and adenomas | Overview & Diagnosis | Diagnosed more frequently recently due to increasing use of abdominal imaging (US and CT) | Commonest benign renal lesions: renal cysts, oncocytomas, angiomyolipomas and renal adenomas | Most often diagnosed accidentally during abdominal imaging (US, CT, MRI) | Symptoms: pain, haematuria and palpable mass | Renal Cysts — Types & Significance | Types | — sporadic; genetic (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease); acquired renal cystic disease (chronic dialysis) | Significance | — exclude malignant cystic lesions | Simple cysts on US | — smooth thin walls and clear fluid content | If malignancy suspected | — contrast-enhanced CT is required | Bosniak Classification | Class | CT Description | Bosniak I | Thin wall, water density, no septation, no calcification, no enhancement | Bosniak II | Thin septa, and/or calcification | Bosniak III | Thick wall or septa with contrast enhancement | Bosniak IV | Cysts with enhancing soft tissue component | Oncocytoma & Angiomyolipoma | Oncocytoma | — most common enhancing benign soft tissue lesion; on CT: hypervascular mass with central scar (not definitively diagnostic); most are surgically removed and diagnosed at histopathology | Angiomyolipoma | — formed of dysmorphic blood vessels, muscle and fat cells; diagnosed by CT detecting the fat component; when large → retroperitoneal haemorrhage; more common in females, more prone to bleeding during pregnancy

Renal Tumors · 2/4 | Renal Cell Carcinoma — Overview & Risk Factors | Overview | 85% of primary malignant renal tumours | 5th & 6th decade of life | 2–3% of all malignant tumours | Male to female ratio 3 : 2 | Pathology — Adenocarcinoma | Gross picture | — common in the upper pole; may fill all the abdomen | Microscopic picture | — clear cell; papillary; chromophobe; collecting duct carcinoma | Spread | — direct; lymphatic; blood | Risk Factors | Smoking | Obesity | Genetic: chromosome 3 and 7 | Von-Hippel-Lindau disease, tuberous sclerosis | Cystic disease of the kidney on dialysis | RCC accounts for 85% of primary malignant renal tumours — usually a disease of the 5th–6th decade with a 3:2 male predominance.

Renal Tumors · 3/4 | RCC Staging — The 2017 TNM Classification | Primary tumour classification | Stage | Definition | TX / T0 | Primary tumour cannot be assessed / no evidence of primary tumour | T1 | 4 cm but ≤ 7 cm | T2 | 7 cm but | 10 cm, limited to the kidney | T3 | Tumour extends into major veins or perinephric tissues but not into the ipsilateral adrenal gland and not beyond Gerota fascia — T3a: renal vein or segmental branches, pelvicalyceal system, perirenal and/or renal sinus fat; T3b: grossly into vena cava below diaphragm; T3c: grossly into vena cava above the diaphragm or invades the wall of the vena cava | T4 | Tumour invades beyond Gerota fascia (including contiguous extension into the ipsilateral adrenal gland) | T-staging separates tumours limited to the kidney (T1–T2), those extending into veins or perinephric tissue within Gerota fascia (T3), and those beyond Gerota fascia (T4).

Renal Tumors · 4/4 | Clinical Picture, Investigations & Treatment | Clinical Picture | Gross hematuria | Loin pain | Palpable mass | Metastasis | Incidental finding | Secondary varicocele | Paraneoplastic syndrome | — Stuffer syndrome, anemia, erythrocytosis, amyloidosis, hypercalcemia | Investigations | Laboratory | — anemia; hematuria with RBCs in urine analysis; ESR | Imaging | — abdominopelvic ultrasonography; multiphase CT scan with contrast of the abdomen and pelvis (renal protocol); magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); chest X-ray and CT scan; metastatic workup | Treatment | Localized RCC | — radical nephrectomy | Metastatic disease | — radiotherapy; chemotherapy; immunotherapy; hormonal therapy; surgery | The classic triad (hematuria, loin pain, mass) is rare today — most tumours are found incidentally on imaging.

05 | Testicular Tumors | The most common genitourinary malignancy in young men (15–35 years) — highly curable, with a 90% cure rate. Germ cell and non-germ cell tumours, staging and multimodal treatment. | URO-ONCOLOGY · SECTION 05

Testicular Tumors · 1/3 | Introduction, Aetiology & Presentation | Introduction | Most common genitourinary tract malignancy in males aged 15–35 | Relatively rare disease — affects less than 1% of all human neoplasms | Only 7% incidence at infancy and teen age, and 7% above 55 years old | More common on the right side | More common in Caucasian than Asian and African populations | Highly curable and treatable — cure rate 90% in all ages | Aetiology | Unknown, but may be cryptorchidism — the commonest risk factor; unfortunately orchiopexy does not prevent cancer | Orchitis and trauma | Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) | Positive family history | Testicular carcinoma in situ | Testicular atrophy | Presentation | Painless scrotal lump | Dull aching pain or heaviness | Acute pain in 10% | — may be due to hemorrhage | Metastasis | Functional — gynecomastia | — in 5% of germ cell tumours

Testicular Tumors · 2/3 | Classification | Germ cell, non-seminomatous germ cell and non-germ cell tumours | Germ Cell Tumours | Derived from semen producing cells | Include seminomas and non-seminomatous germ cell tumours | Seminoma | 70% confined to the testes; 40% incidence | Radio- and chemo-sensitive | Classic | — 80% | Spermatocytic | — best prognosis; 50% above 50 years old | Anaplastic | — higher rate of local recurrence and metastasis with bad prognosis | Non-Seminomatous Germ Cell Tumours — Main Four Types | Yolk sac tumors | — most common in infancy; alpha fetoprotein (AFP) elevated in 90% of cases | Embryonal carcinoma | — smallest germ cell tumours; 40% less than 2 cm; highly malignant | Teratoma | — can contain bone, cartilage, or intestinal tissues | Choriocarcinoma | — commonly presents with metastasis; worst prognosis; human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) elevated in all cases | Non-Germ Cell Tumours | Sertoli cell tumours | Leydig cell tumours

Testicular Tumors · 3/3 | Diagnosis, Staging & Treatment | TNM classification adapted from UICC 2016, 8th edition | Diagnosis | Ultrasonography — scrotal duplex ultrasound | Computed tomography with contrast of the chest, abdomen and pelvis (to detect lymph nodes and other distant metastases) | Positron emission tomography (PET) scan | Treatment | Start with ipsilateral radical orchiectomy | Radiotherapy | Chemotherapy | Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection | pT — Primary Tumour Staging | Stage | Definition | pTx / pT0 | Cannot be assessed / no evidence of primary tumour (e.g., histological scar in testis) | pTis | Intratubular germ cell neoplasia (carcinoma in situ) | pT1 | Limited to testis and epididymis without vascular/lymphatic invasion; may invade tunica albuginea but not tunica vaginalis | pT2 | Limited to testis and epididymis WITH vascular/lymphatic invasion, or extension through tunica albuginea with involvement of tunica vaginalis | pT3 | Invades spermatic cord with or without vascular/lymphatic invasion | pT4 | Invades scrotum with or without vascular/lymphatic invasion

URO-ONCOLOGY | Uro-Oncology — Key Takeaways | Prostate cancer: most common solid neoplasm in Europe; PSA, DRE and TRUS-guided biopsy diagnose; Gleason score grades 2–10; hormonal therapy acts via the LHRH–LH–testosterone–DHT axis; treatment is stage-dependent (T1: surveillance/surgery/RT — T2: radical prostatectomy is standard). | Bladder cancer: painless hematuria in ~85%; urothelial carcinoma is most common; WHO 2004 grading; spread via en bloc (~60%), lymphatic (obturator 74%) and vascular routes (liver 38%); NMIBC → TURBT + intravesical therapy; MIBC → radical cystectomy + pelvic lymphadenectomy. | 90%; radical nephroureterectomy with bladder cuff is the gold standard; endoscopic therapy for solitary kidney, bilateral disease or low-grade lesions; MVAC or gemcitabine + taxanes for advanced disease. | Renal tumors: benign lesions (cysts — Bosniak I–IV, oncocytoma, angiomyolipoma) are increasingly incidental; RCC = 85% of malignant renal tumours; 2017 TNM (T1 ≤ 7 cm, T4 beyond Gerota); localized → radical nephrectomy; metastatic → multimodal therapy. | Testicular tumors: most common GU malignancy at 15–35 years; cryptorchidism is the commonest risk factor; seminoma (40%) vs NSGCT (yolk sac, embryonal, teratoma, choriocarcinoma); treatment starts with ipsilateral radical orchiectomy ± chemo/RT/RPLND — cure rate 90%. | Genitourinary oncology demands accurate staging before therapy — stage drives every treatment decision.

01 | Stone Disease | Urinary stones affect 10–20% of the population with a 50–60% recurrence within 10 years. Supersaturation, nucleation and crystal retention drive stone formation — management spans conservative care, ESWL, PCNL and surgery. | STONES & INFECTIONS · SECTION 01

Stone Disease · 1/16 | Definition & Incidence | Definition | A urinary stone is a crystalline aggregate of different amounts of urinary crystals and an organic matrix | Urinary stones are polycrystalline aggregates of crystalloids and an organic matrix | Incidence | Urolithiasis affects 10–20% of the population | Males are 1–2 times more affected than females | Calculus disease is the 3rd most common urinary tract disease | High recurrence rate of 50–60% within 10 years of the first attack | The single most striking feature of stone disease is its recurrence — over half of patients form a new stone within a decade.

Stone Disease · 2/16 | Pathophysiology — Supersaturation & Crystal Formation | Precipitation occurs when urine becomes supersaturated; crystals may flow out or be retained in renal tubules, promoting aggregation | Three Levels of Saturation | Undersaturated | — stones can be dissolved, and aggregation cannot occur | Saturated (metastable) | — nucleation and crystal growth may occur, but inhibitors can prevent crystallization | Supersaturated | — inhibitors are rendered ineffective and nucleation will occur | Theories of Stone Formation | Nucleation | — due to supersaturation of urine with crystals — homogenous (spontaneous) or heterogenous (epitaxy — growth on a different crystal surface) | Matrix initiation | — urine proteins provide a framework for deposition of crystals | Absence of inhibitors | — decreased concentration of mucoproteins, citrate, pyrophosphate and magnesium | Supersaturation is influenced by urinary pH, ionic strength, solute concentration, and complexation. Most urinary stones form in the renal tubules and migrate downward; exceptions occur when stones form in stagnant urine pools, e.g., in a bladder diverticulum.

Stone Disease · 3/16 | Types & Incidence of Stones | Classification by anatomical site, opacity on plain X-ray, or composition | Composition-Based Classification | Calcium stones | — calcium oxalates and calcium phosphates — 70–80% | Infected stones | — struvite and appetite stones — 10–20% | Uric acid stones | — 5–10% | Cystine stones | — 1–2% | Miscellaneous | — xanthine, silicate, matrix, indinavir stones and others — less than 5% | Basis of Classification | Anatomical site — e.g., renal, ureteric, bladder, urethral | Opacity on plain X-ray — radiolucent (e.g., uric acid, invisible on plain X-ray, requiring ultrasonography or non-enhanced CT) or radiopaque | Composition — the five main groups | Stone Types — Appearance & Radiography | Stone | Appearance / properties | X-ray | Ca oxalate monohydrate | Smooth, dark, very hard | Highly radio-opaque | Ca oxalate dihydrate | Lighter colour, granular surface, easier to fragment | Less radio-opaque | Calcium phosphate | Smooth, yellowish-white; forms in alkaline urine | Radio-opaque | Struvite (ammonium magnesium phosphate) | Alkaline urine, grows rapidly, friable, yellowish-white | Radio-opaque | Uric acid | Forms in acidic urine, yellowish-grey | Radiolucent

Stone Disease · 4/16 | Precipitating Factors & Causes by Stone Type | Precipitating Factors | 1 — Geography (location, climate and seasonal factors) | 2 — Water intake | 3 — Diet | 4 — Metabolic and endocrinal factors | 5 — Infection | 6 — Urine stasis | 7 — Congenital anomalies | Cystine Stones | Autosomal recessive malabsorption abnormality of dibasic amino acids (cysteine, lysine, arginine) in renal tubules | Calcium Stones — Causes | 1 — Hypercalcemia | — hyperparathyroidism, excess vitamin D intake, metastatic bone deposits | 2 — Hypercalciuria | — most common cause — prolonged immobilization, or idiopathic | 3 — Hyperoxaluria | — endogenous or exogenous | 4 — Hypocitraturia | — reduced urinary inhibitors | 5 — Hyperuricosuria | — increased uric acid excretion | Uric Acid Stones — Causes | Hyperuricemia | — in gout, neoplastic disease, and cytotoxic drug intake, etc. | Hyperuricosuria | — due to uricosuric drugs, salicylates, or thiazides

Stone Disease · 5/16 | Complications of Urinary Stones | The Four Major Complications | Obstruction | — leading to back pressure changes that can endanger renal function | Infection | — with its sequelae | Deterioration | — of renal function | Chronic irritation | — that can lead to metaplasia and/or malignant transformation | Clinical Consequence Chain | Stone → obstruction → hydronephrosis → back-pressure nephropathy. Stone + infection → pyonephrosis (an emergency). Chronic irritation of the urothelium by a long-standing stone may trigger metaplasia and, rarely, malignant transformation.

Hematuria | — due to stone migration, superadded infection or malignant change | c. Fever | — due to infection | d. Renal swelling | — due to hydronephrosis or pyonephrosis; or a mass due to malignant transformation | e. Others | — gastrointestinal, uremic manifestations, retarded growth | Urinary Bladder Calculi | a. Irritative | — frequency, urgency and painful micturition | b. Obstructive | — interrupted stream or even urine retention due to stone impaction at the bladder neck | c. Hematuria | — due to injury of mucosa, infection or malignant transformation | Urethral Calculi | a. Voiding symptoms | — weak and interrupted urine stream, or urine retention and painful micturition | b. Palpable stone | — the stone can be palpated along the urethra

Stone Disease · 7/16 | Investigations — Laboratory | Routine Laboratory Panel | Urine analysis | Renal functions | Liver functions | Complete blood picture | Blood sugar | Bleeding and clotting profile | Purpose | The panel screens for metabolic derangements (hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, diabetes), detects infection and haematuria, and assesses renal function and operability (bleeding and clotting profile before any intervention).

Stone Disease · 8/16 | Investigations — Radiology | a — Plain X-Ray of the Urinary Tract (KUB) | Used to diagnose radio-opaque and soft tissue shadows | Differential diagnosis of a radio-opaque shadow on KUB: | Urinary stones · gall bladder stones · phleboliths · appendicolith and foreign bodies in GIT · nephrocalcinosis, calcified renal cysts or tumour · calcified mesenteric lymph nodes · chip fracture of the transverse process or a rib | b — Ultrasonography | Can delineate radiolucent stones | Gives an idea about backpressure changes, associated pathology and echogenicity of renal parenchyma | c — Non-Enhanced CT | Used in diagnosis of stones of the urinary tract whether radio-opaque or radiolucent | Spiral CT is the gold standard for detecting almost all types of stones | d — Other Investigations | IVP, enhanced CT, MRI and renogram — if further information is needed for proper management | MRI | — used if radiation needs to be avoided (e.g., pregnancy) | Renogram (MAG3 or DTPA) | — assesses renal function and drainage

Stone Disease · 10/16 | Intervention — Indications & Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL) | Indications for Intervention | Failed conservative treatment | 1 cm | Increasing backpressure changes | Deterioration of renal functions | Unresolved or persistent UTI | Associated pathology needing intervention | ESWL — Principle | High-energy electricity-generated acoustic shock waves | Focused to the stone using X-ray (C-arm), ultrasonography, or both | The stone is fragmented into minute particles | Conservative treatments are maintained to facilitate passage of stone particles | Indication: stones 2 cm or less | Contraindications of ESWL | Urological | — associated pathology requiring intervention; acute episode of UTI; distal obstruction; larger stones; renal insufficiency; single renal unit unless stented | Non-urological | — pregnancy; bone deformities that render localization of the stone difficult; uncontrollable bleeding diathesis | Advantages & Disadvantages of ESWL | Advantages | — non-invasive; relatively painless; suitable for risky patients; successful for most urinary calculi | Disadvantages | — transient hematuria; colicky pain; fever; Stein-Strasse (multiple small stone fragments obstructing the ureter); failure to disintegrate hard stones (e.g., calcium oxalate monohydrate and cystine stones)

Stone Disease · 11/16 | Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy (PCNL) | The Procedure | Insertion of a ureteric catheter through cystoscopy | A puncture needle punctures the desired calyx through skin under radiographic or ultrasound control | A guide wire is inserted through the puncture needle | The tract is dilated with different types of dilators to accommodate the Amplatz sheath | The nephroscope is passed; forceps and lithotripter probes are used under vision | Small stones removed in toto with stone forceps; larger stones fragmented by lithotripsy (ultrasonic, laser or electrohydraulic) | A nephrostomy tube is left for 1–2 days at the end | Indications | 2 cm | Associated pathology that can be manipulated by the percutaneous route, e.g., PUJO | ESWL failure | Staghorn stones — PCNL can be started with, then ESWL used for small residual stones | Contraindications | Uncontrollable bleeding diathesis | Congenital anomalies rendering the pelvicalyceal system not amenable to the percutaneous route | During pregnancy | Advantages & Disadvantages | Advantages | — small endoscopic wound; lesser post-operative pain; short hospital stay | Disadvantages | — iatrogenic trauma to other organs (colon, duodenum, spleen or pleura); intra- or post-operative bleeding; intra- or extra-peritoneal extravasation; residual stones

Stone Disease · 12/16 | Open Surgery & Management of Ureteric Calculi | Open Surgery | Indicated only if ESWL and PCNL have failed, are contraindicated, or are not available | Nowadays, only about 5% of patients will be candidates for open surgery | Pain Distribution of Ureteric Stones | Upper (proximal) third | — flank pain with referred pain to the testicle | Lower (distal) third | — flank pain, right/left lower quadrant pain, with radiation of pain to the scrotum or vulva | Management by Site | Site | Options (in order) | Upper third | 1 — ESWL; 2 — Ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy; 3 — open surgery | Middle third | 1 — Ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy; 2 — ESWL; 3 — open surgery | Lower third | 1 — Ureteroscopy; 2 — ESWL; 3 — open surgery | Complications of Ureteroscopy | Iatrogenic trauma | Haematuria | Infection | Ureteric stricture

Stone Disease · 13/16 | Management of Bladder & Urethral Stones | Bladder Stones | A — Endoscopically | — crushed mechanically by lithotrite (litholapaxy) or disintegrated by lithotripsy (ultrasonic, laser or electrohydraulic) | B — Open surgery (cystolithotomy) | — indicated in: 1 — large stones that cannot be manipulated endoscopically; 2 — multiple or very hard bladder stones; 3 — bladder diverticular stones; 4 — pediatric bladder calculi especially in absence of laser lithotripsy; 5 — associated pathology needing open surgery | Urethral Stones — Management Depends on Location | Stones of the prostatic urethra | — a metal dilator or an endoscope is used to dislodge the stone into the bladder, and then it is managed as a bladder stone | Anterior urethral stones | — removal of a small stone by urethral forceps through urethroscopy; if this fails, open surgery is indicated | Bladder and urethral stones are managed endoscopically whenever possible; open surgery is reserved for large, hard, diverticular or pediatric stones.

Stone Disease · 14/16 | Metabolic Work-up | Investigations to identify the underlying metabolic cause | Investigations to Perform | A — Serum | — calcium and phosphorus (to exclude hyperparathyroidism); uric acid (to exclude gout) | B — 24-hour urine collection | — for calcium, uric acid, oxalate, and citrate | Normal values (for a 60 kg adult): Calcium 300 mg, uric acid 800 mg, oxalates 40 mg, citrates 300–900 mg. | General Advice to Prevent Recurrence | High fluid intake | Restriction of excess dietary salts | Restriction of excess proteins | Avoid obesity | Stone-Specific Prevention | Calcium oxalate calculi | — minimize diet rich in oxalates; hydrochlorothiazide 50 mg bid; citrates 5 gm bid | Uric acid calculi | — avoid diet rich in purines; rule out myeloproliferative or neoplastic diseases; keep urine alkaline, e.g., sodium bicarbonate 1 gm t.d.s.; allopurinol 100–300 mg/day in hyperuricaemia | Infected stones | — long-term antibiotic suppressive therapy; avoid or minimize indwelling catheters and stents whenever possible

STONES & INFECTIONS | Stone Disease — Key Takeaways | Stones are polycrystalline aggregates; recurrence reaches 50–60% within 10 years — the 3rd most common urinary tract disease. | Formation requires supersaturation; inhibitors (citrate, magnesium, pyrophosphate, mucoproteins) protect; pH and ionic strength modulate solubility. | Calcium stones dominate (70–80%); uric acid stones are radiolucent; struvite stones signal infection. | Diagnosis: KUB (radio-opaque), US (radiolucent), non-enhanced/spiral CT is the gold standard; renogram (MAG3/DTPA) assesses function and drainage. | Management ladder: conservative ( | 2 cm, staghorn) → open surgery (about 5% of patients); ureteric stones are treated per site with ureteroscopy ± laser or ESWL. | Metabolic work-up (serum calcium/phosphorus/uric acid + 24-h urine calcium, uric acid, oxalate, citrate) guides recurrence prevention. | Prevention of recurrence is as important as stone removal — metabolic evaluation and advice follow every treatment.

02 | Urinary Tract Infections | UTIs are among the most prevalent infectious diseases and represent about 40% of all hospital-acquired infections. From significant bacteriuria and pathogenesis to treatment of uncomplicated, complicated and special-group infections. | STONES & INFECTIONS · SECTION 02

Urinary Tract Infections · 1/13 | Introduction & Significant Bacteriuria | The gold standard for diagnosis is detection of the pathogen in the presence of clinical symptoms | Burden of Disease | Among the most prevalent infectious diseases, with a substantial financial burden on society | Represent about 40% of all hospital-acquired infections | In the USA: over 7 million physician visits annually, including more than 2 million visits for cystitis | Approximately 15% of all community-prescribed antibiotics are dispensed for UTI — estimated annual cost over US $1 billion (Naber et al., EAU 2010) | Diagnosis & Bacteriuria Thresholds | Gold standard: detection of the pathogen (urine culture, midstream urine) in the presence of clinical symptoms; this also estimates the level of bacteriuria | 10⁵ cfu/mL) in pyelonephritis of pregnancy (Kass, 1960) | Acute uncomplicated cystitis (women) | 10³ cfu/mL of uropathogens in MSU | Acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis (women) | 10⁴ cfu/mL in MSU | Complicated UTI | 10⁴ cfu/mL (men, or straight catheter urine in women) | Suprapubic bladder puncture | — any count of bacteria is relevant | MSU = mid-stream sample of urine; cfu = colony-forming units.

Urinary Tract Infections · 2/13 | Evaluation | History — The First Step | Effective management begins with a careful history | Attention to: current symptomatology; prior episodes of documented UTI; risk factors that can initiate a UTI (e.g., urethral catheterization or sexual intercourse) | Risk factors that can complicate a UTI: diabetes mellitus or pregnancy | Specimen Collection | A midstream voided specimen is generally adequate | Urethral catheterization or suprapubic aspiration may be necessary in an individual who cannot produce a clean specimen | Urinalysis — Pyuria & Bacteriuria | UTI is a host inflammatory response to bacterial invasion | Urinalysis reveals pyuria — the presence of white blood cells in the urine — and bacteriuria | If there is bacteriuria with no pyuria in an asymptomatic patient: an infection is not present, and therapy is usually not necessary | Key Clinical Point | Bacteriuria without pyuria in an asymptomatic patient is not infection — asymptomatic bacteriuria generally does not require therapy.

Urinary Tract Infections · 3/13 | Pathogenesis | Route of infection, pathogens and virulence factors | Causative Pathogens | Escherichia coli is the most common — 85% of infections in ambulatory patients and 50% of nosocomial infections | Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Enterococcus faecalis are the next most frequent isolates | Most infections: retrograde ascent of bacteria from the fecal flora via the urethra to the bladder and kidney | Catheter-Related Infection | A single catheter insertion in ambulatory patients results in a UTI in 1–2% of cases | Indwelling catheters with open-drainage systems lead to bacteriuria in nearly 100% of patients within 3–4 days | Hematogenous Infection | Restricted to a few relatively uncommon microbes that cause primary infections elsewhere in the body: | Staphylococcus aureus | Candida sp. | Salmonella sp. | Mycobacterium tuberculosis | Virulence & Host Factors | Urinary pathogen virulence factors promote adherence to mucosal surfaces | Bacteria usually express fimbriae or pili which mediate adherence to epithelial cell receptors | Host factors such as epithelial cell receptivity are also important | E. coli binds more avidly to vaginal epithelial cells from women with recurrent UTIs than from healthy individuals (Fowler et al., 1977)

Urinary Tract Infections · 4/13 | Classification | Uncomplicated UTI · Complicated UTI · Urosepsis | The Three Clinical Categories | 1 — Uncomplicated UTI | 2 — Complicated UTI | 3 — Urosepsis | Uncomplicated UTIs in Adults | Include episodes of acute cystitis and acute pyelonephritis in otherwise healthy individuals | The spectrum of etiological agents is similar in uncomplicated upper and lower UTIs | E. coli is the causative pathogen in 70–95% of cases | Staphylococcus saprophyticus in 5–10% | What Makes a UTI Complicated? | Structural or functional abnormalities of the urinary tract | Indwelling catheters, stents or instrumentation | Obstructive uropathy | Renal insufficiency, transplantation, diabetes, immunodeficiency | Vesicoureteral reflux and other functional abnormalities | Urinary tract modifications (ileal loop or pouch) | The uncomplicated/complicated distinction drives both investigation and antimicrobial choice.

Urinary Tract Infections · 5/13 | Acute Uncomplicated Cystitis (Premenopausal, Non-Pregnant Women) | When Are Urine Cultures Recommended? | Suspected acute pyelonephritis | Symptoms that do not resolve or recur within 2–4 weeks after completion of treatment | Microbiological Diagnosis | 10³ cfu/mL is microbiologically diagnostic | Treatment | Regimen | Dose | Duration | Cotrimoxazole | 160/800 mg bid | 3 days | Trimethoprim | 200 mg | 5 days | Alternative: ciprofloxacin | 250 mg bid | — | Short 3-day cotrimoxazole is the classic first-line; ciprofloxacin is an alternative when resistance or intolerance applies.

Urinary Tract Infections · 6/13 | Acute Uncomplicated Pyelonephritis (Premenopausal, Non-Pregnant Women) | Diagnosis & Imaging | 10⁴ cfu/mL | Ultrasound should be performed to rule out urinary obstruction or renal stone disease | 3 days: computed tomography or (DMSA) scan are indicated to rule out urolithiasis, renal or perinephric abscesses | Imaging for persistent pyelonephritis: CT, excretory urogram, or DMSA scan | Treatment | Mild cases (first line) | — oral fluoroquinolone for 7 days | Severe cases | — hospital admission; parenteral fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin) or a third-generation cephalosporin | Continuation | — treatment continued for 1–2 weeks with oral antibiotics | Pyelonephritis is a systemic infection: imaging excludes obstruction and abscess; severe cases require parenteral therapy in hospital.

Urinary Tract Infections · 7/13 | Recurrent UTIs in Women & UTIs in Pregnancy | Recurrent (Uncomplicated) UTIs in Women | Long-term, low-dose prophylactic antimicrobials taken at bedtime | Prophylactic alternative methods: immunotherapy and probiotic therapy | Acidification, and cranberry juice | UTIs in Pregnancy — Key Facts | Most symptomatic UTIs in pregnant women present as acute cystitis | Prevalence of asymptomatic bacteriuria: 4–7% (American, European and Australian studies); 20–40% of women with asymptomatic bacteriuria develop pyelonephritis during pregnancy | Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria lowers this risk | Pregnancy — Treatment | Recurrent UTI prophylaxis | — low-dose cephalexin (125–250 mg) or nitrofurantoin (50 mg) daily at night | Acute pyelonephritis | — second or third generation cephalosporins, an aminoglycoside, or an aminopenicillin plus a beta-lactam inhibitor (BLI) | Contraindicated in 1st trimester | — quinolones, tetracyclines and TMP | Complicated UTI in pregnancy | — if right hydronephrosis occurs with a UTI, a ureteral stent may be indicated to drain urine; antimicrobial prophylaxis continued until delivery | In pregnancy, treat asymptomatic bacteriuria — it prevents progression to pyelonephritis.

Urinary Tract Infections · 8/14 | UTIs in Post-Menopausal Women | Evaluation of Recurrent UTI | In cases of recurrent UTI, a urological or gynaecological evaluation should be performed | Purpose: rule out underlying causes — tumors, obstructive problems, detrusor failure, or genital infections | Treatment | Intravaginal oestriol therapy has been shown to significantly reduce the rate of recurrence in post-menopausal women with recurrent UTIs | Oestriol restores the vaginal flora and epithelium, reducing the reservoir of uropathogens.

Urinary Tract Infections · 9/13 | Recurrent UTI — Subclassification & Factors Suggesting Complicated UTI | Recurrent UTI — Three Groups | 1 — Unresolved infection | — subtherapeutic level of antimicrobial; non-compliance with treatment; malabsorption; resistant pathogens | 2 — Bacterial persistence | — may be due to a nidus for persistent infection in the urinary tract; surgical correction or medical treatment for urinary dysfunction may be needed | 3 — Reinfection | — each episode is a new infection acquired from periurethral, perineal or rectal flora | Factors Suggesting a Potential Complicated UTI | Indwelling catheter, stent or splint (urethral, ureteral, renal) or intermittent bladder catheterization | 100 mL | Obstructive uropathy of any aetiology — e.g., bladder outlet obstruction (including neurogenic bladder), stones and tumour | Vesicoureteric reflux or other functional abnormalities | Urinary tract modifications — ileal loop or pouch | Renal insufficiency and transplantation, diabetes mellitus and immunodeficiency | Unresolved = never cleared; persistence = same site, same organism; reinfection = new episode from the perineal/rectal reservoir.

Urinary Tract Infections · 10/13 | Catheter Fever & Sepsis Syndrome in Urology (Urosepsis) | Catheter Fever — General Aspects | 1 — Written catheter care protocols are necessary | 2 — Health care workers should observe protocols on hand hygiene and use disposable gloves between catheterized patients | 3 — An indwelling catheter should be introduced under antiseptic conditions | 4 — Urethral trauma minimized by adequate lubricant and small catheter calibre | 5 — The duration of catheterization should be minimal | Urosepsis | SIRS (fever or hypothermia, hyperleucocytosis or leucopenia, tachycardia, tachypnoea) is the first event in a cascade to multi-organ failure | Sepsis or septic shock may follow | The prognosis of urosepsis is globally better than sepsis from other infectious sites | Mortality rate as high as 20–40% | Treatment of Urosepsis | Adequate life-supporting care | Appropriate and prompt antibiotic therapy | Adjunctive measures — sympathomimetic amines, hydrocortisone, blood glucose control, recombinant activated protein C | Optimal management of urinary tract disorders

Urinary Tract Infections · 12/13 | Prostatitis, Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome & Epididymo-Orchitis | NIDDK/NIH Classification of Prostatitis | I | — Acute bacterial prostatitis | II | — Chronic bacterial prostatitis | III | — Chronic abacterial prostatitis — chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CPPS): A. inflammatory CPPS (white cells in semen/EPS/VB3); B. non-inflammatory CPPS (no white cells) | IV | — Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis (histological prostatitis) | Treatment of Prostatitis | Acute bacterial prostatitis | — admission and parenteral antibiotics, then oral for 2–4 weeks | Chronic prostatitis | — ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin are drugs of choice because of their favourable pharmacokinetic properties (4–6 weeks) | Epididymitis & Orchitis | Complications of epididymo-orchitis: abscess formation, testicular infarction, testicular atrophy, chronic epididymal induration and infertility | Antimicrobials should be selected on an empirical basis | Chlamydia | — doxycycline, 200 mg/day | Gram-negative organisms | — fluoroquinolones | EPS = expressed prostatic secretion; VB3 = post-massage urine sample. 01 | Urinary Incontinence | Any involuntary loss of urine. Stress, urge, mixed, overflow, continuous, nocturnal and transient types — each with distinct mechanisms, risks and management strategies. | FUNCTIONAL UROLOGY & ANDROLOGY · SECTION 01

Urinary Incontinence · 1/12 | Definition & Consequences | Any involuntary loss of urine | Definition | Any involuntary loss of urine | Consequences of Incontinence | Urinary tract infection (UTI) | Depression and poor self-esteem | Restricts physical activity | Falls and fractures | Negative effect on sexual activity; interpersonal relationships suffer | Why It Matters | Incontinence is not merely a bothersome symptom — it is a driver of infection, psychological distress, social withdrawal and physical injury (falls and fractures). Its impact on sexual function and relationships compounds the disability, so active diagnosis and treatment are essential.

Urinary Incontinence · 2/12 | Types — Stress, Urge, Mixed & Overflow | Stress Incontinence | Involuntary loss of urine on exertion, sneezing, or coughing | Risk factors | — obesity; pregnancy; vaginal delivery and obstructed labor; menopause; chronic cough & constipation; smoking; prior pelvic surgery | Urge Incontinence | Involuntary loss of urine accompanied by or immediately preceded by urgency | Incontinence related to an involuntary detrusor contraction | Mixed Incontinence | Combined stress and urge urinary incontinence | Overflow Incontinence | Leakage of urine associated with urinary retention (bladder over-distension)

Urinary Incontinence · 3/12 | Types — Continuous, Nocturnal, Post-Micturition & Pharmacologic | Continuous Urinary Incontinence | Continuous leakage of urine | Most common causes | — 1 — urinary fistulas; 2 — ectopic ureter | Nocturnal Enuresis & Post-Micturition Dribbling | Nocturnal enuresis | — loss of urine occurring during sleep | Post-micturition dribbling | — involuntary loss of urine immediately after passing urine | Pharmacologic Urinary Incontinence | Loss of urine due to effect of medications taken by the patient | Diuretics | — do not cause incontinence but may exacerbate incontinence symptoms | Anticholinergics | — may impair bladder emptying | Tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., imipramine) | — may increase bladder outlet obstruction and contribute to urinary retention and overflow incontinence | Doxazosin or tamsulosin | — may cause or worsen stress incontinence | A medication review is a mandatory step — drugs may cause or unmask incontinence.

Urinary Incontinence · 4/12 | Types — Transient Incontinence | Reversible causes that should be identified and corrected first | Delirium & Psychological Causes | Delirium | Psychological factors — e.g., severe depression or neurosis | Excessive Urine Output | High fluid intake | Diuretics | Metabolic abnormalities — hyperglycaemia, hypercalcemia | Fluid overload — congestive heart failure, peripheral venous insufficiency, hypoalbuminemia | Drug-induced peripheral oedema — calcium channel blockers, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) | Amantadine (drug for Parkinson disease and influenza) | Beta blockers | Stool Impaction | Stool impaction can precipitate transient incontinence — treat the impaction before further evaluation | Clinical Approach | Transient causes are reversible: delirium, psychological illness, excessive urine output and stool impaction. Correcting them may cure the incontinence without any further therapy.

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia · 1/10 | Anatomy of the Prostate | Gross Anatomy | Approximately 70% glandular elements and 30% fibromuscular stroma | Normal prostate weighs 18 g; measures 3 cm in length, 4 cm in width, and 2 cm in depth | Traversed by the prostatic urethra | Ovoid shape with anterior, posterior and 2 inferolateral surfaces; narrowed apex inferiorly and broad base superiorly | Zonal Anatomy | A — Anterior (ventral) fibromuscular stroma | — fibrous, non-glandular | B — Glandular portion | — 1 — peripheral zone: about 70% of the glandular part; 2 — central zone: about 25% of the glandular prostate; 3 — transition zone and periurethral glands | BPH arises predominantly in the transition zone and periurethral glands — the zone that surrounds the prostatic urethra.

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia · 2/10 | Incidence & Epidemiology | Incidence | BPH is the most common benign tumour in men | Pathological incidence about 30% in men above forty | Clinical incidence about 40% in men above fifty, increasing 10% each decade | Epidemiology | Ethnic background | — prostate enlargement is less common in Asian men than in white and black men | Diabetes and heart disease | — diabetes, heart disease and use of beta blockers might increase the risk of BPH | Lifestyle | — obesity increases the risk; exercise lowers the risk | Heredity | Autosomal dominant inheritance in approximately 50% of men undergoing prostatectomy for BPH when younger than 60 years | Only about 9% of men undergoing prostatectomy when older than 60 years would be predicted to have familial risk | Familial BPH characterized by large prostate size: mean volume 82.7 mL (hereditary) vs 55.5 mL (sporadic)

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia · 4/10 | Pathology & Pathophysiology | The cascade from prostatic enlargement to renal impairment | 1 — Prostate Obstruction | Obstruction by: two lateral lobes · median lobe · three lobes · or small fibrous type | 2 — Urethral Obstruction | Through bilateral compression and elongation of the prostatic urethra | 3 — Bladder Changes | Compensatory hypertrophy of detrusor muscles | Decompensatory stage: atrophy of the muscles, saccules and diverticula | 4 — Upper Tract Dilatation | Ureter and kidney dilatation — the endpoint of chronic obstruction

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia · 5/10 | Symptoms & the AUA Symptom Score | Symptoms | Obstructive | — hesitancy, weak stream, forked, intermittent stream and post-micturition dribbling | Irritative | — urgency, frequency — especially at night first, then day and night, precipitancy, and lastly urge incontinence | Complications | — of chronic obstruction | AUA Score — Interpretation | Total score runs from 0 to 35 points | 0–7 points | — mildly symptomatic | 8–19 points | — moderately symptomatic | 20–35 points | — severely symptomatic | The Seven AUA Questions | 1 — Frequency | 2 — Urgency | 3 — Nocturia | 4 — Weak stream | 5 — Intermittent micturition | 6 — Straining | 7 — Incomplete emptying | The AUA symptom index quantifies severity (0–35) and guides the choice between watchful waiting, medical and surgical therapy.

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia · 6/10 | Examination & Investigations | Examination | General and abdominal examination — specially to exclude signs of straining (hernia) or uremic manifestations | DRE | — smooth, firm, elastic enlargement of the prostate; preservation of the median sulcus and exaggeration of the two lateral sulci; induration, if detected, must alert the physician to the possibility of cancer | Focused neurological examination, especially anal tone | Investigations | Urine analysis | Serum creatinine | Serum PSA | Ultrasound | Plain X-ray, intravenous urography (I.V.U.) or CT with or without contrast in some cases with associated pathology or complications | Uroflowmetry and urodynamic profiles, especially in suspected neurological element | Cystoscopy in cases with suspected bladder mass | DRE + PSA remain the key cancer-screening elements in the BPH work-up.

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia · 7/10 | Differential Diagnosis & Complications | Differential Diagnosis | Other obstructive conditions of the lower urinary tract: urethral stricture, bladder neck contracture, bladder stone, prostate cancer | Urinary tract infection | Neurogenic bladder disorders — either spastic or flaccid types | Complications | STASIS | INFECTION | STONE FORMATIONS | HEMATURIA | ACUTE RETENTION | CHRONIC RETENTION | CHRONIC RETENTION WITH OVERFLOW | RENAL FAILURE | The complication list is a progression: stasis begets infection and stones, retention follows, and renal failure is the ultimate threat.

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia · 8/10 | Treatment — Watchful Waiting & Medical Therapy | Watchful Waiting | Instructions to the patient to avoid: cold weather; excessive fluid intake; sexual excitement; some drugs — diuretics, antispasmodics and alpha-adrenergic stimulants (as common cold drugs) | Medical Therapy | Alpha-adrenergic blockers | — relax bladder neck muscles and muscle fibres in the prostate, making urination easier; alfuzosin, doxazosin; more specific alpha-1 blockers: tamsulosin, silodosin; usually work quickly in men with relatively small prostates | 5-alpha-reductase enzyme inhibitors | — prevent conversion of testosterone to the more active dihydrotestosterone; shrink prostate size by about 25%; finasteride and dutasteride (more potent); may take three to six months to be effective | Phosphodiesterase (PDE) 5 inhibitors | — tadalafil (Cialis) — used for erectile dysfunction, can also treat prostate enlargement through relaxation of smooth muscles | Combination therapy | — combined alpha-blocker + 5-ARI | Phytotherapy | — acts as anti-inflammatory and decongestant | Treatment of any UTI | — always address infection | Alpha-blockers act quickly; 5-ARIs shrink the gland over months — combination therapy serves larger prostates.

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia · 9/10 | Surgical & Minimally Invasive Therapy | Surgical Therapy | Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) — unipolar or better bipolar resection; the gold standard technique for surgical management | Transurethral incision of the prostate — in small fibrous glands | Transurethral laser prostatectomy — vaporization or enucleation | Transurethral microwave hyperthermia | Transurethral needle ablation of the prostate | High-intensity focused ultrasound | Intraurethral stents | Transurethral balloon dilation of the prostate | Open prostatectomy — trans-vesical or retropubic approach | Heat Therapies (Minimally Invasive) | Destroy prostate tissue with heat; tissue is left in the body and expelled over time (called sloughing) | Transurethral Microwave Therapy (TUMT) | Transurethral Needle Ablation (TUNA®) | Interstitial Laser Coagulation (ILC) | Water Induced Thermotherapy (WIT) | Possible Side Effects of Heat Therapies | Urinary tract infection | Impotence | Incontinence | TURP remains the gold standard; laser enucleation and minimally invasive heat therapies broaden the armamentarium.

Male Infertility · 1/8 | Definition, Hormonal Axis & Spermatogenesis | Definition & Incidence | Inability to conceive after 1 year of unprotected sexual intercourse | 15% of couples suffer from infertility after one year | 40% of cases due to male factor, 40% female factor, 20% both male and female factors | Testis Function | Endocrine | — testosterone: 2% free, 98% bound to sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG); estrogen and thyroid hormone decrease SHBG and increase free T; androgen, growth hormone and obesity decrease free T | Exocrine | — sperm | Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis | Hypothalamus secretes gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) | GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete gonadotropins: FSH and LH | FSH stimulates spermatogenesis in the testes; LH stimulates testosterone (T) production | Testosterone has a negative feedback effect on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland | Spermatogenesis | Blood-testis barrier: the strongest intercellular barrier in the body — tight junctions between Sertoli cells | Germ cells: spermatogonia; primary spermatocytes; secondary spermatocytes; spermatids | Total time to produce a sperm: 42–76 days (varies widely among individuals) | Phases: a — proliferative (mitotic) phase; b — meiotic phase (reduction division → haploid spermatids); c — spermiogenesis (metamorphosis into mature spermatozoa)

Male Infertility · 2/8 | Causes of Male Infertility — Pretesticular | Disorders of the hypothalamus and pituitary | Hypothalamic Disease | Gonadotropin deficiency — Kallmann syndrome | Isolated LH deficiency — fertile eunuch | Isolated FSH deficiency | Congenital hypogonadotropic syndrome | Pituitary Disease | Pituitary insufficiency — tumour, infiltrative disease, surgical removal, radiation, or metastatic deposits | Hyperprolactinemia | Exogenous hormones — oestrogen/androgen excess, glucocorticoid excess, or hyper- and hypothyroidism | Pre-testicular causes are hormonal — the testis itself is normal but lacks gonadotropic drive.

Male Infertility · 3/8 | Causes of Male Infertility — Testicular | Testicular Causes | Chromosomal — e.g., Klinefelter syndrome | Noonan syndrome (male Turner syndrome) | Myotonic dystrophy | Vanishing testis syndrome (bilateral anorchia) | Sertoli cell only syndrome (germ cell aplasia) | Y chromosome microdeletion | Gonadotoxins (radiation, drugs) | Systemic diseases — renal failure, liver failure, sickle cell disease | Defective androgen activity | Testis injury — orchitis, torsion, trauma | Cryptorchidism | Varicocele | Idiopathic | Medications Associated with Infertility | Inhibit T synthesis | — ketoconazole, spironolactone, alcohol | Androgen antagonist | — cimetidine | Lower T levels | — marijuana, heroin, methadone | Oestrogen-like activity | — pesticides | Gonadotoxic | — chemotherapy | Others | — calcium channel blockers; sulfasalazine; colchicine; allopurinol; alpha-blockers; nitrofurantoin; antipsychotics; antidepressants | Varicocele is the most common surgically correctable cause; Klinefelter the archetypal chromosomal cause.

Male Infertility · 4/8 | Causes of Male Infertility — Post-Testicular | Reproductive Tract Obstruction | Congenital absent vas (CAV) | Ejaculatory duct obstruction | Idiopathic obstruction of the epididymis | Vasectomy | Groin surgery | Infection | Sympathetic injury (spinal cord trauma, or pelvic surgery) | Disorders of Sperm Motility | Immotile cilia syndrome | Infection | Disorders of Coitus | Impotence | Hypospadias | Obstruction is surgically correctable in many cases (vasovasostomy, epididymovasostomy, TURED).

Male Infertility · 6/8 | Laboratory Tests & Semen Analysis | WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen (5th edition) | Laboratory Tests | Urinalysis | Semen analysis — collection after 48–72 hours of sexual abstinence | Seminal fructose and post-ejaculate urinalysis — fructose is derived from the seminal vesicle | Hormone assessment: FSH, LH and testosterone | Minimum Criteria for Adequate Semen Analysis | Parameter | Lower reference | Semen volume (mL) | 1.5 | Total sperm number (10⁶/ejaculate) | 39 | Sperm concentration (10⁶/mL) | 15 | Total motility (PR + NP) | 40 | Progressive motility (PR, %) | 32 | Vitality (live spermatozoa, %) | 58 | Sperm morphology (normal forms, %) | 4

Male Infertility · 7/8 | Radiologic Testing & Medical Treatment | Radiologic & Special Testing | Scrotal ultrasound, transrectal ultrasound | CT scan or MRI of the pelvis | Testis biopsy & vasography | Fine-needle aspiration 'mapping' of the testes | Semen culture | Empiric Medical Therapy | Clomiphene citrate: antiestrogen; increases secretion of GnRH, FSH and LH | Antioxidant therapy: vitamin E | Medical Treatment | Pyospermia | — evaluate for sexually transmitted diseases, penile discharge, prostatitis, or epididymitis | Coital therapy | — timing and technique counselling | Autoimmune infertility | — corticosteroid therapy, sperm washout, or assisted reproductive techniques (IUI, IVF, ICSI) | Hormonal disturbances | — treatment of hyperprolactinemia, hypothyroidism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and testosterone excess/deficiency | Hormonal abnormalities and infection are treated first; empiric therapy (clomiphene, antioxidants) follows when no cause is found.
