Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 1/13 | Erectile Dysfunction — Definition, Epidemiology & Risk Factors | Definition | The persistent inability to attain and maintain an erection sufficient to permit satisfactory sexual performance | Epidemiology | Worldwide prevalence 10–20% of adult males (older than 20 years) | Increases with age: 1–10% below 40 years; 50–100% between 70 and 90 years | Risk Factors | Age | Diabetes mellitus | Cardiovascular diseases | Hypertension | Smoking | Overweight | Cardiovascular Warning | Established evidence: the presence of ED increases the risk of future cardiovascular events — myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular events, and cardiovascular mortality | ED is a marker of vascular health — it often precedes overt cardiovascular disease.

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 2/13 | Erectile Dysfunction — Etiology | Psychogenic | Life stressors, and/or conflict with partner | Performance anxiety | Vasculogenic | Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, hypertension, obesity, lack of exercise, diabetes mellitus, radiotherapy to the pelvis | Neurogenic & Hormonal | Neurogenic | — diabetes mellitus, stroke, spinal cord trauma, pelvic and urethral surgeries | Hormonal | — diabetes mellitus, hypogonadism, panhypopituitarism | Drug-Induced & Anatomical | Drug induced | — antihypertensives (thiazide, beta-blockers), antidepressants, antiandrogens, recreational drugs (heroin, cocaine, excessive alcohol) | Anatomical | — Peyronie's disease, penile fracture, vascular trauma

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 3/13 | Erectile Dysfunction — Diagnosis | History Taking | Detailed medical and sexual history | Onset and course of ED | Validated questionnaires — international index of erectile function (IIEF) | Other sexual problems: decreased libido, premature ejaculation | Co-morbidities: diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular problems | Laboratory Evaluation | Fasting blood sugar and lipid profile | Morning total testosterone level — if clinical suspicion of hypogonadism | If total testosterone is low: free testosterone, luteinizing hormone (LH) and prolactin should be measured | Focused Physical Examination | Genital examination: penile deformities, size of the testis | Prostate examination: size of prostate and prostate cancer | Signs of hypogonadism | Cardiovascular and neurological examination | Advanced Workup (not routine) | Nocturnal penile tumescence and rigidity test (NPTR) | — measures number and rigidity of erection episodes at night; differentiates organic from psychogenic ED | Duplex ultrasound of the penis | — measures blood flow velocity; normal values exclude vasculogenic ED | Penile arteriography | — indicated after trauma to the penis or perineum, or suspected pudendal artery stenosis, in patients prepared for penile revascularization surgery

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 4/14 | Erectile Dysfunction — Management | General Principles | Identify and treat curable causes — hypogonadism, psychogenic factors | Risk factors and lifestyle modifications: weight reduction, control of diabetes mellitus and hypertension, smoking cessation, regular exercise | Oral Pharmacotherapy — PDE5 Inhibitors | Sildenafil, tadalafil, avanafil, vardenafil | Inhibit catalysis of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) in the cavernosal tissue | cGMP accumulation → vasodilation with enhanced blood flow in the penile cavernosal tissue | Common side effects: headache, flushing, nasal congestion, myalgia, back pain | Contraindicated with organic nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide mononitrate, isosorbide dinitrate) — the combination causes severe hypotension | Treatment Ladder at a Glance | 1 — Treat curable causes + lifestyle modification | 2 — Oral PDE5 inhibitors (first line) | 3 — Topical alprostadil (cream or pellets) | 4 — Intracavernosal injection (alprostadil) | 5 — Vacuum erection devices (VED) | 6 — Penile prosthesis (definitive therapy) | PDE5 inhibitors work by preserving cGMP — never combine with organic nitrates (severe hypotension).

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 5/14 | Erectile Dysfunction — Second-Line & Definitive Options | Topical Alprostadil | Vasodilator effect; applied topically as cream or pellets | Adverse effects — creams | — erythema, temporary burning or pain | Adverse effects — pellets | — local pain, dizziness and hypotension, urethral bleeding | Intracavernosal Injection | Vasoactive substances, e.g., alprostadil — effective in 70% of cases | Side effects | — pain (50%), prolonged erections (5%), priapism (1%), penile fibrosis (2%) | Vacuum Erection Devices (VED) | Provide passive engorgement of the corpus cavernosum, with a constrictor ring placed at the base of the penis to retain blood within the corpus | Most common adverse events | — pain, inability to ejaculate, petechiae, bruising, numbness | Penile Prosthesis | Considered in patients who prefer a definitive therapy, or who do not respond to or have side effects from pharmacological therapies | Two types | — semi-rigid and inflatable | Complications | — infection, mechanical failure, erosion of corpora, urethra or glans penis | The treatment ladder: PDE5 inhibitors → topical → injection → VED → prosthesis.

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 6/14 | Premature Ejaculation — Definition, Classification & Causes | International Society of Sexual Medicine 2014 | Definition (ISSM 2014) | 1 — Ejaculation that always or nearly always occurs prior to or within 1 minute of vaginal penetration (lifelong PE), or a clinically significant and bothersome reduction in latency time, often to about 3 minutes or less (acquired PE) | 2 — Inability to delay ejaculation on all or nearly all vaginal penetrations | 3 — Negative personal consequences: distress, bother, frustration, and/or avoidance of sexual intimacy | Prevalence & Classification | Prevalence | — varies from 5–30% of the male population | Lifelong (primary) PE | — manifests from the first sexual encounter | Acquired (secondary) PE | — develops at some point in life after a previous normal ejaculation experience | Variable PE | — irregular (or situational) early ejaculation — considered normal | Subjective PE | — perceived early ejaculation with normal ejaculation time | Causes | Lifelong PE | — hyposensitivity of the 5-HT2c and/or hypersensitivity of the 5-HT1a receptor | Acquired PE | — sexual performance anxiety; psychological and relationship problems; erectile dysfunction; prostatitis; hyperthyroidism; during recreational drugs withdrawal | Serotonergic receptor sensitivity (5-HT2c / 5-HT1a) underlies lifelong PE — the rationale for SSRI therapy.

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 6/13 | Premature Ejaculation — Evaluation & Management | Evaluation | History taking | — full sexual history: erectile function, ejaculation time, sexual satisfaction of patient and partner; full medical history: co-morbidities and medications; validated questionnaires, e.g., Index of Premature Ejaculation | Physical examination | — lifelong PE: little to find; acquired PE: examine for signs of inflammation — urethritis, or prostatitis (tender prostate during DRE) | Investigations | — no routine investigations unless examination reveals a suspected underlying cause (erectile dysfunction, endocrinopathy such as hyperthyroidism, or infections) | Management | Treat the cause | — in secondary PE — e.g., erectile dysfunction, prostatitis, or hyperthyroidism | Psychological & behavioural | — relieve patient anxiety; sexual behavioural therapy, e.g., start-stop technique | Pharmacotherapy (SSRIs) | — dapoxetine — the only FDA approved pharmacotherapy for PE; on demand 30–60 mg one hour before sexual intercourse; daily paroxetine 10–40 mg/day, or citalopram 20–40 mg/day | Local anaesthetics | — lidocaine and/or prilocaine as spray, gel or cream — effective in delaying ejaculation; can be used alone or combined with oral pharmacotherapy | Start-stop technique + on-demand dapoxetine is the classic combined approach.

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 7/13 | Urethritis & Gonococcal Infection | Aetiology of Urethritis | Gonococcal | — Neisseria gonorrhoea (5–20%) | Non-gonococcal | — Chlamydia trachomatis (15–40%); Mycoplasma genitalium (15–25%); Trichomonas vaginalis; Ureaplasma urealyticum; herpes simplex virus; adenovirus | N. gonorrhoea — Clinical Presentation | Incubation period 3–14 days | Males: purulent urethral discharge, dysuria, urethral itching | May progress to epididymitis, orchitis or prostatitis | Proctitis with anal intercourse | Females: often asymptomatic; sequelae — pelvic inflammatory disease and tubal scarring | About 450,000 cases of gonorrhoea were diagnosed in 2016 | Pathology & Diagnosis | Gram-negative diplococcus that lives intracellularly | Gram stain of male urethral discharge/swab: polymorphonuclear leukocytes with gram-negative intracellular diplococci — diagnostic | Culture of urethral specimen if swab negative | NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) on urethral swab or first-catch urine — quicker and more sensitive; the preferred diagnostic tool nowadays | Positive patients should be screened also for other STIs: chlamydia, syphilis and HIV | Treatment — CDC Recommendations | Single dose of ceftriaxone 250 mg IM + azithromycin 1 g orally | Alternative: single dose of cefixime 400 mg orally + azithromycin 1 g orally | Cephalosporin allergy: single dose of azithromycin 1 g orally + gemifloxacin 320 mg orally or gentamicin 240 mg IM | Abstain from sexual activity for 7 days after treatment | All sexual partners within 60 days before the date of infection should be referred for evaluation | Follow-up test to confirm cure at 3–4 months after treatment

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 9/16 | Chlamydia, Mycoplasma genitalium & Trichomonas | Chlamydia trachomatis | Accounts for 15–40% of non-gonococcal urethritis; more common in younger men | Incubation period 3–14 days | NAATs using first-catch urine are the most sensitive test in men | Positive patients screened also for gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV | Treatment | — azithromycin 1 g orally single dose, or doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, or erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days, or levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily for 7 days, or ofloxacin 300 mg orally twice daily for 7 days | Trichomonas vaginalis | Flagellated parasite infecting male and female urethra, and female vulva and vagina | Rates vary by geographical area: 2–13% | Diagnosis: NAAT; should be screened for in areas with high prevalence | Treatment | — metronidazole 2 g orally once, or tinidazole 2 g orally once | Mycoplasma genitalium | 15–20% of non-gonococcal urethritis cases | 30% of cases of recurrent or persistent urethritis | NAAT is the only available diagnostic test | Should be suspected in recurrent or persistent urethritis | Treatment | — azithromycin 1 g orally single dose; resistant cases: moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7, 10 or 14 days | Recurrent or persistent urethritis after treatment should prompt evaluation for Mycoplasma genitalium.

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 10/14 | Genital Ulcers — Herpes Simplex Virus | Causes of Genital Ulcers | Herpes simplex virus | Syphilis | Chancroid | Donovanosis | Pathology | HSV type 1 and type 2 are double-stranded DNA viruses | Infects epithelial cells and nerve endings, then travels through nerve axons to reach sacral ganglia and reside there in a latent stage | Reactivation triggers: trauma, ultraviolet light, immunosuppression, fever | Clinical Picture & Complications | Painful papules progressing to vesicles, then ulcer with local lymphadenitis | Possible complications: aseptic meningitis and autonomic dysfunction resulting in urinary retention | Diagnosis | Cell cultures and PCR of swabs taken from the base of the genital ulcer are the recommended diagnostic tool | Treatment | Acyclovir 400 mg orally three times a day for 7–10 days, OR | Acyclovir 200 mg orally five times a day for 7–10 days, OR | Valacyclovir 1 g orally twice a day for 7–10 days, OR | Famciclovir 250 mg orally three times a day for 7–10 days

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 11/16 | Syphilis — Clinical Presentation | Treponema pallidum — a coiled spiral spirochete bacterium; ~10.6 million incident cases annually | Latent Syphilis | Defined as seroreactivity with no clinical evidence of disease | Tertiary Syphilis | About 35% of individuals with late latent syphilis develop the late manifestations: neurosyphilis, cardiovascular syphilis, and gummatous syphilis | The four-stage course: primary chancre → secondary bacteremia/rash → latent → tertiary. | Primary Syphilis | Development of an ulcer (chancre), usually with regional lymphadenopathy | The chancre is usually painless, single, and indurated, with a clean base discharging clear serum | Incubation period between contact and chancre: 10–90 days | Secondary Syphilis | Arises from bacteremia that usually occurs 3–5 months after the initial infection | Maculopapular rash involving the palms of the hands and soles of the feet; mucous membrane lesions involving the vagina or anus | The rash can ulcerate and lead to condyloma lata (large, raised gray or white lesions) | Additional symptoms: fever, lymphadenopathy, alopecia, weight loss

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 12/16 | Syphilis — Diagnosis & Treatment | Diagnosis | Darkfield examination of lesion exudate can detect Treponema pallidum | Non-treponemal serology | — venereal disease research laboratory test (VDRL); rapid plasma reagin test (RPR) | Treponemal serology | — fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test (FTA-ABS); T. pallidum particle agglutination test (TP-PA) | Diagnosis of syphilis requires two laboratory serologic tests: a non-treponemal test and a treponemal test | Treatment | Intravenous penicillin G is the preferred drug for treating all stages of syphilis | Key Teaching Points | Non-treponemal tests (VDRL, RPR) are screening tests; treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TP-PA) confirm | Both test types together establish the diagnosis | Penicillin G covers all stages — primary, secondary, latent and tertiary | Darkfield microscopy is the direct diagnostic method; serology is the mainstay of screening and confirmation.

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 12/14 | Chancroid | Treatment | Regimen | Dose | Azithromycin | 1 g in a single dose | Ceftriaxone | 250 mg IM in single dose | Ciprofloxacin | 500 mg orally twice per day for 3 days | Erythromycin base | 500 mg orally three times per day for 7 days | Probable diagnosis: painful ulcers with negative syphilis and HSV work-up — treat empirically. | Etiology | Caused by the gram-negative bacterium Haemophilus ducreyi | Infection leads to anogenital ulceration and lymphadenitis with progression to bubo formation | Diagnosis | A definitive diagnosis of chancroid requires culture on media not routinely available | The CDC suggests a probable diagnosis can be made if the patient has one or more painful ulcers with no evidence of T. pallidum or HSV infection

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 14/16 | Human Papillomavirus — Genital Warts | Etiology | Double-stranded DNA virus of the Papillomaviridae family | More than 100 types exist; more than 40 types can infect the genital area and be sexually transmitted | Types 6 and 11: non-oncogenic — responsible for about 90% of anogenital warts | Types 16 and 18: cervical cancer and other anogenital cancers (vulvar, vaginal, anal, penile) | Pathology & Diagnosis | Pathology | — infection starts at the basal cell layer of stratified squamous epithelium, stimulating cell proliferation; Bowenoid papulosis — reddish-brown verrucous papules on the penis, a low-grade carcinoma in situ; giant condyloma acuminatum — large verrucous exophytic lesions, associated with HPV-6 or HPV-11 | Diagnosis | — warts seen clinically; latent viruses detectable only through demonstration of HPV DNA in skin or mucosa; biopsy from lesions to rule out malignancy | Treatment — Removal, Not Cure | Goal: removal of the warts — treatment will not eradicate the infection | Patient-applied | — podofilox 0.5% solution or gel; imiquimod cream 5%; sinecatechins 15% ointment | Provider-administered | — podophyllin resin 10–25% in tincture of benzoin; cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen); trichloroacetic acid; surgical therapy — direct excision, shaving, curettage, or laser ablation | Types 6/11 cause warts; types 16/18 drive anogenital cancers.

Sexual Dysfunction & STDs · 14/14 | Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) | Virology & Transmission | HIV is a retrovirus that infects T cells and dendritic cells | Spread through blood, semen, vaginal fluid, or breast milk | Immunosuppression occurs with the progressive loss of CD4 T-lymphocytes | Diagnosis | Serologic tests detect antibodies against HIV-1 and HIV-2; virologic tests detect HIV antigens or RNA | ELISA testing of serum detects antibodies against HIV antigens | The second confirmatory test is western blot | Three Recognized Stages | Stage 1 — Acute | — occurs 2–4 weeks after infection; flu-like symptoms; patients at increased risk of transmitting the virus; routine HIV antibody tests are often negative during this phase | Stage 2 — Clinical latency | — slow viral replication lasting years to decades depending on treatment; patients often asymptomatic | Stage 3 — AIDS | — diagnosed when the CD4 count is less than 200 cells/mm³ | Treatment — ART / HAART | Antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses HIV replication | Standard: combination of drugs (highly active antiretroviral therapy — HAART) to increase potency and reduce the likelihood of resistance | ART reduces mortality and morbidity and improves quality of life | Drug classes: nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), protease inhibitors (PIs), integrase inhibitors (INSTIs)

FUNCTIONAL UROLOGY & ANDROLOGY | Erectile Dysfunction & Premature Ejaculation — Key Takeaways | ED: persistent inability to attain and maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory performance; prevalence 10–20% rising to 50–100% at 70–90 years; risk factors — age, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, smoking, overweight; ED predicts future cardiovascular events. | ED etiology: psychogenic, vasculogenic (atherosclerosis, diabetes, pelvic radiotherapy), neurogenic (diabetes, stroke, spinal trauma, pelvic surgery), hormonal (hypogonadism, panhypopituitarism), drug-induced (thiazides, beta-blockers, antidepressants, antiandrogens, recreational drugs), anatomical (Peyronie's disease, penile fracture). | ED diagnosis: history + IIEF; physical — genital, prostate, hypogonadism, cardiovascular/neurological; labs — fasting glucose, lipids, morning testosterone, LH/prolactin if low; NPTR differentiates organic from psychogenic; penile duplex and arteriography in selected cases. | ED management: treat curable causes; lifestyle modification; PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, avanafil, vardenafil) — contraindicated with organic nitrates; then topical alprostadil, intracavernosal injection (effective 70%; priapism 1%), vacuum devices, and penile prosthesis. | PE (ISSM 2014): ejaculation within ~1 minute of penetration (lifelong) or ~3 minutes (acquired), inability to delay ejaculation, negative personal consequences; lifelong PE — 5-HT2c hyposensitivity/5-HT1a hypersensitivity; classification — lifelong, acquired, variable, subjective. | PE management: treat the cause (ED, prostatitis, hyperthyroidism); psychological/behavioural (start-stop technique); dapoxetine 30–60 mg on demand — the only FDA-approved drug; daily paroxetine or citalopram; local anaesthetics (lidocaine/prilocaine). | ED is a vascular warning sign; PE responds to behavioural therapy, SSRIs and local anaesthetics.

FUNCTIONAL UROLOGY & ANDROLOGY | Sexually Transmitted Diseases — Key Takeaways | Urethritis: gonococcal (N. gonorrhoea 5–20%) vs non-gonococcal (chlamydia 15–40%, Mycoplasma 15–25%, trichomonas, ureaplasma, HSV, adenovirus); gram stain with intracellular diplococci is diagnostic; NAAT is preferred. | Gonorrhoea (CDC): ceftriaxone 250 mg IM + azithromycin 1 g orally single dose (or cefixime 400 mg + azithromycin); abstain 7 days; treat partners from the preceding 60 days; test of cure at 3–4 months. | Chlamydia: azithromycin 1 g single dose or doxycycline 100 mg bid × 7 days; Mycoplasma genitalium: azithromycin 1 g, moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for resistant cases; Trichomonas: metronidazole or tinidazole 2 g single dose. | Genital ulcers: HSV (acyclovir 400 mg tds or 200 mg 5×/day, valacyclovir 1 g bid, famciclovir 250 mg tds × 7–10 days), syphilis (chancre → rash → latent → tertiary; VDRL/RPR + FTA-ABS/TP-PA; IV penicillin G for all stages), chancroid (H. ducreyi; azithromycin 1 g, ceftriaxone 250 mg IM, ciprofloxacin 500 mg bid × 3 days, erythromycin 500 mg tds × 7 days), donovanosis. | HPV warts: types 6/11 cause ~90% of anogenital warts; 16/18 cause anogenital cancers; treatment removes warts but does not eradicate the virus (podofilox, imiquimod, sinecatechins; cryotherapy, TCA, excision, laser). | HIV: retrovirus infecting T cells and dendritic cells; stages — acute (2–4 weeks, flu-like, antibodies often negative), clinical latency, AIDS (CD4 | Screen, treat and trace partners — STI control depends on completing the chain of transmission.

01 | Anatomy of the Urinary Tract | From the embryological development of the kidney to the surgical anatomy of the scrotum — structure, relations, blood supply and innervation that underpin every urological procedure. | BASICS & RENAL · SECTION 01

Anatomy · 1/12 | Embryology — Development of the Kidneys | Three successive kidney stages, from cranial to caudal | The Three Kidney Stages | Pronephros | — rudimentary, non-functional; represented by nephrotomes | Mesonephros | — functional intermediate kidney with mesonephric tubules and mesonephric duct (Wolffian duct); develops beside the subcardinal and posterior cardinal veins; glomerular capsule and glomerulus form | Metanephros | — the definitive kidney — develops from the interaction of the ureteric bud (outgrowth of the mesonephric duct) with the metanephrogenic blastema (uninduced intermediate mesoderm) | Key Developmental Events | The ureteric bud branches to form the collecting system — calyces, pelvis, ureter | The metanephrogenic blastema forms the nephrons | Cloaca | — receives the allantois, hindgut, mesonephric ducts and ureteric buds | Urorectal septum | — divides the cloaca into the urogenital sinus (ventral → bladder and urethra) and the anal canal (dorsal → hindgut) | Bladder trigone | — the mesonephric ducts and ureteric buds are progressively incorporated into the bladder wall; ureteric orifices migrate cranially/laterally while mesonephric duct openings move caudally (toward the urethra in males → ejaculatory ducts) | Differentiation of External Genitalia | Indifferent stage (7–9 weeks) | — genital tubercle, urogenital sinus, genital folds, genital swellings | Male (12 weeks → late fetus) | — formation of the penis, urethral groove, and scrotum (genital swellings fuse) | Female (12 weeks → late fetus) | — formation of the clitoris, labia majora/minora, and urethral and vaginal orifices

Anatomy · 2/12 | The Kidneys — Overview | Position & Size | Lie obliquely along the borders of the psoas muscles | The right kidney is lower than the left (displaced by the liver) | Adult kidney weighs about 150 g; measures ~12 × 6 × 3 cm (left often slightly longer) | Extend from T12 to L3; the hilum lies at L1 | Bean-shaped, indented medially (the renal sinus) | Each kidney contains about one million nephrons (glomerulus + tubules) | Support | Perirenal fat | Renal vascular pedicle | Abdominal muscle tone | Bulk of the abdominal viscera | The kidney and its strong capsule are surrounded by pararenal fat | Internal Structure | Outer cortex and inner medulla | Medulla: multiple medullary pyramids, each opening through its tip into a minor calyx | Minor calyces → three major calyces (upper, middle, lower) → renal pelvis → ureter | Renal lobe | — a medullary pyramid plus its overlying cortex | Columns of Bertin | — extensions of cortical tissue between the pyramids | Renal papilla | — the tip of a pyramid that projects into a minor calyx

Anatomy · 3/12 | Renal Hilum, Pelvis & Renal Fascia | Renal Hilum (at the concave part of each kidney) | 1 — Renal vein exits (anteriorly) | 2 — Renal artery enters (posterior to the renal vein) | 3 — Renal pelvis exits (posterior to the artery) | Renal Pelvis | Funnel-shaped; lined with transitional epithelium with a smooth muscle and connective tissue wall | Continuous inferiorly with the ureter | Divides into major and minor calyces | Urine flow: collecting tubule → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureters → bladder | Renal (Gerota's) Fascia | Encloses the kidney with its surrounding fibrous and fatty capsules | Helps maintain organ position | Superiorly: continuous with the fascia of the inferior diaphragm | Medially: the left and right fascia blend with each other anterior to the abdominal aorta and IVC | Posterior layer blends with the fascia overlying the psoas | The hilum arrangement — vein anterior, artery middle, pelvis posterior — is a classic examination question.

Anatomy · 4/12 | Relations, Blood Supply & Innervation | Relations of the Kidneys | Posterior surface | — superiorly: diaphragm, pleura and lower two ribs; inferiorly (medial to lateral): psoas major, quadratus lumborum, transversus abdominis | Right kidney anterior | — right suprarenal gland, liver, second part of the duodenum, right colic flexure, coils of small intestine | Left kidney anterior | — left suprarenal gland, stomach, spleen, pancreas, left colic flexure and descending colon, jejunum | Vessels & Lymphatics | Arterial | — renal arteries branch from the aorta at L1/L2 behind the pancreas and renal veins; enter at the hilum: anteriorly — apical, upper, middle, lower segments; posteriorly — posterior segment; no communication between segments | Venous | — renal veins communicate widely, eventually forming 5 vessels that unite at the hilum; drain into the IVC | Lymphatic | — para-aortic nodes at L1/L2; the surface of the upper kidney drains through the diaphragm into posterior mediastinal nodes | Innervation | Sympathetic: preganglionic cells in spinal cord T12/L1 → fibres to thoracic and lumbar splanchnic nerves | Postganglionic cells in coeliac, renal and superior hypogastric plexuses | Vasomotor function

Anatomy · 5/12 | The Adrenal Glands | Overview | Each kidney is capped by an adrenal gland | Enclosed within Gerota's (perirenal) fascia | Each adrenal weighs about 5 g | Right adrenal is triangular; left adrenal is more rounded and crescentic | Each gland: cortex — chiefly influenced by the pituitary gland; medulla — derived from chromaffin tissue | Relations | Right adrenal lies between the liver and the vena cava | Left adrenal lies close to the aorta; covered on its lower surface by the pancreas; superiorly and laterally related to the spleen | Arterial Supply | Three arteries: one from the inferior phrenic artery, one from the aorta, and one from the renal artery | Venous Drainage & Lymphatics | Right adrenal vein drains into the inferior vena cava | Left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein | Lymphatic vessels accompany the suprarenal vein and drain into lumbar lymph nodes | The left adrenal vein → left renal vein is the key landmark for adrenal surgery.

Anatomy · 6/12 | The Ureter | Course | Continue from the renal pelvis at the level of L1 | Each ureter is about 25 cm long | Runs inferomedially along the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae | Crosses the pelvic brim at the SIJ, anterior to the origins of the external iliac artery | Runs anterior to the internal iliac artery in the pelvis | Passes towards the ischial spine, then turns towards the pubic tubercle and enters the bladder | In females | — the uterine arteries cross the juxtavesical portion of the ureters | In males | — the vasa deferentia sweep over the lateral pelvic walls anterior to the ureters, lying medial to them before joining the seminal vesicle | Ureteral Landmarks (Radiologic) | UPJ — ureteropelvic junction (where the renal pelvis joins the ureter) | UVJ — ureterovesical junction (where the ureter enters the bladder) | Iliac vessels — the landmark where the ureter crosses into the pelvis | UO — ureteral orifice | On retrograde pyelography the ureter is divided into three segments (I, II, III) corresponding to the abdominal and pelvic portions | Blood Supply & Lymphatics | Supplied along its course by: aorta, renal arteries, gonadal arteries, common iliac, internal iliac, vesical and uterine arteries | Lymphatics | — upper ureter → lumbar nodes; middle → internal iliac (hypogastric) and common iliac nodes; lower → vesical and hypogastric nodes

Anatomy · 7/13 | The Urinary Bladder — Structure & Trigone | Structure | Hollow muscular reservoir; capacity 400–500 mL in the adult | In women, the posterior wall and dome are invaginated by the uterus | Wall layers: outer — loose connective tissue; middle — smooth muscle and elastic fibres (detrusor); inner — transitional epithelium (urothelium) | Histologic layers (inside out): mucosa (epithelium), submucosa (lamina propria), muscle (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer deep longitudinal), subserosa/perivesical fat, peritoneum | The intramural ureter travels obliquely within the smooth muscle layer — the oblique course provides an anti-reflux mechanism | Trigone & Ureterovesical Junction | The ureter enters the bladder through the ureteral hiatus | Superficial trigone: the smooth white zone of mucosa; deep trigone: the muscular layer continuous with the ureteric sheath | Waldeyer sheath: a longitudinal muscle layer of the distal ureter that continues into the deep trigone | The trigone: triangular area on the bladder floor formed by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice (bladder neck) | The bladder and ureter are related to the urachus (remnant of the allantois) at the bladder apex

Anatomy · 8/13 | The Urinary Bladder — Vessels & Innervation | Arterial Supply & Venous Drainage | Arterial | — superior, middle and inferior vesical arteries from the anterior trunk of the internal iliac (hypogastric) artery; smaller branches from obturator and inferior gluteal arteries; in females, uterine and vaginal arteries also send branches | Venous | — rich plexus surrounding the bladder, emptying into the internal iliac (hypogastric) veins | Lymphatics | Drain into the vesical, external iliac, internal iliac (hypogastric), and common iliac lymph nodes | Innervation | Pelvic nerves: sensory nerves detect the degree of stretching in the bladder wall | Parasympathetic motor nerves then cause contraction of the bladder | Somatic nerves (pudendal) control the voluntary skeletal muscle of the external sphincter | Sympathetic nerves stimulate the bladder neck and external sphincter during filling (contraction); this is inhibited during micturition | Spinal cord levels: sympathetic outflow T11–L2; parasympathetic (S2–S4) and pudendal nerve (S2–S4) | Sensory → parasympathetic → somatic (pudendal) → sympathetic: the four players of bladder storage and emptying.

Anatomy · 8/12 | The Prostate Gland & Urethra | Prostate — Overview | Fibromuscular and glandular organ lying just inferior to the bladder | Normal prostate weighs about 20 g; contains the posterior urethra (~2.5 cm in length) | Supported anteriorly by the puboprostatic ligaments and inferiorly by the urogenital diaphragm | Perforated posteriorly by the ejaculatory ducts, which open into the verumontanum on the floor of the prostatic urethra | Lowsley classification: 5 lobes — anterior, posterior, median, right lateral, left lateral | McNeal (1972): peripheral, central and transitional zones; an anterior segment; and a preprostatic sphincteric zone | Prostate — Vessels, Nerves & Relations | Arterial | — inferior vesical, internal pudendal and middle rectal (hemorrhoidal) arteries | Venous | — periprostatic plexus, connected with the deep dorsal vein of the penis and internal iliac (hypogastric) veins | Nerves | — rich supply from sympathetic and parasympathetic plexuses | Lymphatics | — internal iliac (hypogastric), sacral, vesical and external iliac nodes | Relations | — lies behind the pubic symphysis; vasa deferentia and seminal vesicles close to its posterosuperior surface; posteriorly separated from the rectum by the two layers of Denonvilliers' fascia | Urethra | Extends from the base of the bladder to the outside world | Female: 4 cm long | Male: 15 cm long

Anatomy · 9/12 | Clinical Relevance of Anatomy | Catheterisation | Female | — short urethra — catheter passes directly into the bladder | Male | — longer urethra passing through the prostate | Suprapubic catheterisation | — needle/catheter inserted through the abdominal wall into the bladder, bypassing the urethra | Digital Rectal Examination (DRE) | The prostate is palpated through the rectal wall | Requires knowledge of the prostate's relation to the rectum — separated by Denonvilliers' fascia | Scrotal Masses — Differentiation Questions | Is it attached to / part of the testicle? | Is it separate from the testicle? | Is it transilluminable? | Can you feel the testicle? | Can you get above the mass? | Common Scrotal Masses | Epididymal cyst | — fluid-filled sac within the epididymis | Indirect inguinal hernia | — abdominal contents pass through the deep inguinal ring | Testicular cancer | — solid tumour within the testicle | Hydrocele | — collection of fluid surrounding the testicle, within the tunica vaginalis

Anatomy · 10/13 | Anatomy of the Scrotum & Spermatic Cord | Testis Descent & Spermatic Cord | The fetal testis descends from the abdomen through the layers of the anterior abdominal wall and the processus vaginalis (peritoneal outpouching) | The layers the testis passes through form the coverings of the spermatic cord and scrotum | Cord coverings: internal spermatic fascia (from transversalis fascia); cremasteric fascia and muscle (from transversus abdominis & internal oblique); external spermatic fascia (from external oblique aponeurosis) | Contents: ductus deferens (45 cm), testicular artery, artery to the ductus deferens, cremasteric artery, pampiniform plexus, sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves, genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, lymphatics | Descent & Its Clinical Legacy | The processus vaginalis is the peritoneal outpouching through which the testis descends | Failure of its obliteration explains indirect inguinal hernia and hydrocele | The coverings of the cord arise from the abdominal wall layers the testis traverses

Anatomy · 11/13 | Layers & Testis Structure | Layers of the Spermatic Cord & Scrotum | 1 — Peritoneum | 2 — Transversalis fascia | 3 — Transversus abdominis & internal oblique | 4 — External oblique | 5 — Subcutaneous fat | 6 — Skin | Testis — Structure | Testes: 4–5 cm long, 3 cm wide, 2.5 cm deep; volume 30 mL | Internal structure (outside in): tunica vaginalis (parietal and visceral layers with the cavity between), tunica albuginea, septa of the testis, seminiferous tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis (head, body, tail), ductus deferens | Testis — Vessels & Lymphatics | Arterial | — internal spermatic artery from the aorta; vasal artery from the internal iliac artery | Venous | — pampiniform plexus of veins → spermatic vein; right spermatic vein enters the vena cava; left spermatic vein enters the left renal vein | Lymphatics | — lymphatic vessels from the testes pass to the lumbar lymph nodes, connected to the mediastinal nodes | Left spermatic vein → left renal vein: the anatomical basis of left-sided varicocele and its renal tumour association.

Anatomy · 11/12 | Scrotal Contents — Summary | Scrotal Contents | Testis covered by the visceral layer of the tunica vaginalis, except where the testis is attached to the epididymis and spermatic cord | Parietal layer attached to the internal spermatic fascia | Fluid between the layers allows movement | Key Anatomical Points | Testis descent through the processus vaginalis explains indirect hernias and hydroceles | Left spermatic vein drains into the left renal vein — the basis of left-sided varicocele and its association with renal tumours | Testicular lymphatics drain to lumbar nodes — testicular cancer metastasizes retroperitoneally, not to inguinal nodes | The oblique intramural ureter is the anti-reflux mechanism of the bladder | Anatomy explains clinical signs: transillumination (hydrocele), 'getting above the mass' (hernia vs testicular lesion), and retroperitoneal spread of testicular cancer.

02 | Congenital Anomalies | Anomalies of number, structure, size, rotation, ascent and fusion of the kidney; duplications and obstruction of the ureter; bladder exstrophy; urethral valves; hypospadias; and the undescended testis. | BASICS & RENAL · SECTION 02

Congenital Anomalies · 1/10 | Kidney — Anomalies in Number | Bilateral Renal Agenesis | Complete absence of the kidneys and ureters, with a definite clinical picture: | Peculiar facial appearance | Pulmonary abnormalities | Often a single umbilical artery | May be caused by failure of formation of either the ureteric bud or the nephrogenic blastema | Incompatible with life | Unilateral Renal Agenesis | Absence of one kidney and ureter | Occurs more frequently than bilateral renal agenesis | Compatible with life if the solitary kidney is intact | Differential Diagnosis on IVU | Ectopic kidney (kidney in an abnormal position) | Non-visualized or obstructed kidney | Renal failure (lack of contrast excretion) | Prior surgical removal (nephrectomy)

Congenital Anomalies · 2/10 | Polycystic Kidney Disease — Adult & Infantile Types | Adult Type (Autosomal Dominant) | More common than the infantile type | Most cases identified between the age of 30 and 50 years | Features | — renal mass, flank pain, haematuria, urinary tract infections, renal insufficiency later in life | Patients are usually managed symptomatically and need dialysis later in life when renal insufficiency develops | Infantile Type (Autosomal Recessive) | Autosomal recessive and very rare | Small cysts representing generalized dilatation of the collecting tubules | 4 types | — perinatal, neonatal, infantile, juvenile | The earlier the age, the more severe the disease and the worse the prognosis | Features | — bilateral; flank pain, renal mass, pulmonary hypoplasia, oliguria, hypertension | If evident at birth: death within the first 2 months; if later: renal failure and hypertension occur more slowly | Adult PKD = autosomal dominant, presents 30–50 years; infantile PKD = autosomal recessive, earlier onset = worse prognosis.

Congenital Anomalies · 3/10 | Kidney — Anomalies of Size, Structure & Rotation | Solitary (Simple) Renal Cysts | Thin-walled cysts and thick-walled cysts (with calcifications) may occur | Diagnostic imaging: contrast medium filling via percutaneous needle puncture and demonstration on renal angiogram | Renal Hypoplasia | Congenitally small kidney | Contains a small number of normal nephrons | Renal function is normal in proportion to the mass of the kidney | May be unilateral or bilateral | Renal Dysplasia | Contains focal, diffuse, or segmentally arranged primitive structures, specifically primitive ducts | A result of abnormal metanephric differentiation | All or only part of the kidney may be affected; the kidney may be abnormal in size or small | Cysts of various types may be present (cystic dysplasia) | The entire kidney may be dysplastic with predominance of cysts (multicystic dysplastic kidney) | Anomalies in Rotation | Failure of rotation during ascent to the renal fossa | The renal pelvis varies in position from medial to other degrees of malrotation | Possible malrotated positions: ventral, ventromedial, dorsal, and lateral

Congenital Anomalies · 8/10 | Cryptorchidism — The Undescended Testis | Definition & Types | Abnormal location of the testis | Dystopic | — the testis has descended but stopped in an abnormal location along the normal path of descent | Ectopic | — the testis has descended into a location completely outside the normal path of descent | Risks & Differential Diagnosis | Risks | — high risk of malignant change; affects spermatogenesis (infertility); susceptible to torsion; susceptible to trauma | Differential diagnosis | — dystopic; ectopic; agenesis; post-surgical removal; vanishing testis syndrome | Not palpable | — posterior abdominal wall (intra-abdominal); inguinal canal | Palpable | — external inguinal ring; groin; neck of the scrotum | Treatment | Before the age of one year | Medical | — hormonal therapy with human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) or gonadotropin-releasing hormone; overall efficacy rate of less than 20% | Surgical — palpable testis | — one-stage orchiopexy | Surgical — non-palpable testis | — examination under anaesthesia: if felt → one-stage orchidopexy; if not felt → diagnostic laparoscopy: if located → one-stage orchiopexy; if short vessels → two-stage orchiopexy (e.g., Fowler–Stephens procedure) | Treat before one year of age; non-palpable testis requires laparoscopy.

Investigations · 1/8 | Urine Analysis — Collection & Macroscopic Examination | Timing of Collection | First-voided morning sample: to avoid orthostatic proteinuria (increase in protein with physical activity) | 24-hour urine collection | — 1 — proteinuria; 2 — renal function tests; 3 — vinyl mandelic acid (VMA); 4 — metabolic workup for stone disease | Method of Collection | 1 — Voided sample | 2 — Catheter specimen | 3 — Suprapubic aspiration in infants | Macroscopic Examination | Colour | — normal: yellow; red — haematuria, haemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria, rifampicin; brown — haematuria, porphyria, jaundice | Aspect | — normal: clear; turbid — infection, phosphaturia | Specific gravity | — normal 1003–1030; fixed at 1010 in chronic renal failure; increased in dehydration; decreased in diabetes insipidus and with diuretics | pH | — normal 5.5–7.5; acidic urine in uric acid stone formers; alkaline urine in infection with urea-splitting organisms | First morning urine avoids orthostatic proteinuria; 24-hour collection is used for proteinuria, renal function, VMA and stone work-up.

Investigations · 2/8 | Urine Analysis — Microscopic Examination | Cells & Casts | RBCs: normal | WBCs: normal | Casts | — protein casts — interstitial nephritis; RBC casts — glomerulonephritis; WBC casts — infection and pyelonephritis; cellular casts — acute tubular necrosis | Crystals, Bacteria & Parasites | Crystals | — oxalate, uric acid, struvite, cystine | Bacteria | — 5 bacteria/hpf indicates 10⁵ colony forming units/mL of urine | Parasites | — bilharziasis and trichomonas | Interpretation at a Glance | Finding | Suggests | RBC casts | Glomerulonephritis | WBC casts | Infection / pyelonephritis | Cellular casts | Acute tubular necrosis | Protein casts | Interstitial nephritis | Bacteria ≥ 5/hpf | ≥ 10⁵ cfu/mL — significant bacteriuria | hpf = high-power field; cfu = colony-forming units.

Investigations · 3/8 | Serum Creatinine & Creatinine Clearance | Uses | Serum creatinine | — indicator for renal function; a rise indicates damage to a significant number of nephrons | Creatinine clearance | — used to estimate glomerular filtration rate (GFR) | Formula | — GFR = Urine creatinine (U) × Urine volume (V) / Plasma creatinine (P) | Normal GFR | — 90–120 mL/min | Normal Values | Adult | — 0.4 – 1.4 mg/dL | Children | — 0.2 – 0.7 mg/dL | Creatinine clearance is the bedside estimate of GFR — the product of urinary concentration and flow divided by plasma level.

Investigations · 4/8 | Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) | Nature & Values | A 34 kD glycoprotein enzyme produced by prostatic epithelial cells | Present in semen to liquefy the ejaculate | Some is absorbed into blood → 75% bound to plasma proteins while 25% is free | Values | — semen level 0.5 to 5 mg/dL; blood level | Factors That Increase PSA in Blood | Prostatitis | Prostate cancer | Enlarged prostate | Urethral catheterization and instrumentations | Prostate biopsy | Derivatives | Free/Total PSA | — if the ratio | PSA velocity | 0.75 ng/mL/yr | PSA density | — serum total PSA divided by prostate volume (ng/mL/gram); cutoff ≥ 0.15 ng/mL/gram | Age-specific PSA | — 40–49 yrs → 0–2.5; 50–59 → 3.5; 60–70 → 4.5; 70–79 → 6.5 | Uses | Screening and early detection of prostate cancer | Follow-up of response to treatment after prostate cancer therapy

Investigations · 5/8 | Plain X-Ray of the Urinary Tract (KUB) | Introduction | KUB may be used as a scout film, to which contrast studies may be compared | Or as a primary survey to assess urologic or abdominal pathologic processes | Typical field of view: kidneys superiorly, bladder inferiorly; also lower ribs, liver, bowel, spleen, lumbar spine, sacrum, bony pelvis | In larger patients two films may be required | A good KUB should show the last 3 ribs and the lower border of the ischial tuberosity | Assessment — Film & Technical Factors | Film specifics | — name of patient; age & date of birth; location of patient; date taken; film number (if applicable) | Technical factors | — type of projection (supine is standard); markings of any special techniques used | Calcified Structures ('White Bits') | Type 1 | — calcium that is an abnormal structure — e.g., gallstones and renal calculi | Type 2 | — calcium within a normal structure, but representing pathology — e.g., nephrocalcinosis | Type 3 | — calcium within a normal structure, but harmless — e.g., lymph node calcification | Soft Tissue & Foreign Bodies | Soft tissue | — kidneys, spleen, liver and bladder (if filled) seen, plus psoas shadows and abdominal fat; poorly seen compared with US or CT — rarely is action taken on this imaging alone | Foreign bodies | — ingested and rectal foreign bodies; items in the x-ray path (belt buckles, buttons, jewellery); deliberately placed objects (aortic stent, IVC filter, suprapubic catheter); sterilization clips and intra-uterine devices in women

Investigations · 6/8 | Intravenous Urography (IVU) | Introduction | Depends on visualization of the urinary tract by injecting contrast medium that is concentrated and excreted by the kidneys, delineating the tract on X-ray | Nowadays its use in urology has diminished due to the availability of cross-sectional imaging such as CT and MRI | Uses | 1 — Obstruction: congenital (UPJO); acquired (ureteric strictures) | 2 — Haematuria | 3 — Recurrent UTIs | 4 — Stone disease | 5 — Urinary tract fistulas | Phases | 1 — Plain film (KUB or scout film) | 2 — Nephrogram (dye concentrated into the kidney parenchyma) | 3 — Urogram (supine film after 5–10 minutes, visualizing the collecting system) | 4 — Prone film (pressure on the abdomen causes fullness of the collecting system with a better contrast image) | 5 — Full bladder film (can detect filling defects in the bladder) | 6 — Post-micturition film (to evaluate bladder emptying) | The six IVU phases progress from scout film through nephrogram, urogram, prone, full bladder and post-micturition films.

AKI · 1/14 | Acute Kidney Injury — Introduction & Definitions | Introduction | Abrupt and usually reversible decline in the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), characterized by progressive azotemia | Assessed via serum creatinine and urine output | AKI — Diagnostic Criteria | Increase in serum creatinine ≥ 0.3 to 0.5 mg/dL within 48 hours | Increase in serum creatinine ≥ 1.5 times baseline within the previous 7 days | Urine volume ≤ 0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6 hours | Decrease in GFR by 25%

AKI · 2/14 | AKI — Renal Function Markers, Oliguria & Anuria | Biochemistry of Renal Function Markers | Urea (BUN) | — a nitrogenous end product of metabolism from dietary and tissue protein turnover | Creatinine | — the product of muscle creatine catabolism | BUN and serum creatinine are screening tests for renal function; primarily handled by glomerular filtration, they do not adapt significantly as renal function declines — they essentially reflect the GFR | Serum creatinine is an insensitive marker influenced by age, muscle mass and medications | Oliguria & Anuria | Oliguria | — urine output | Anuria | — urine output | Clinical pearl | — abrupt onset of anuria typically suggests bilateral urinary obstruction or catastrophic bilateral kidney injury | AKI patients can be classified as oliguric or non-oliguric — this classification has prognostic value | Creatinine reflects GFR because it is handled almost entirely by filtration; urea adds dietary and catabolic load.

AKI · 2/13 | Stages of Acute Kidney Injury (KDIGO) | Stage | Serum creatinine | Urine output | Stage I | 0.3 mg/dL increase | Stage II | 2–2.9 times baseline | Stage III | 4 mg/dL, or initiation of renal replacement therapy (dialysis) | Staging by the worst criterion (creatinine OR urine output); Stage III includes the need for dialysis.

AKI · 3/14 | Aetiology of AKI — Pre-Renal & Intrinsic | Pre-Renal (55%) | Adaptive response to volume depletion and hypotension; nephrons remain structurally intact | Hypovolemia | Decreased cardiac output: CHF, liver failure | Drugs affecting renal auto-regulation: NSAIDs, ACE-I/ARBs, cyclosporin | Renal / Intrinsic (40%) | Caused by cytotoxic, ischemic, or inflammatory insults leading to structural and functional damage | Glomerular | — acute glomerulonephritis | Tubular / interstitium | — ischemia, sepsis, nephrotoxic drugs | Vascular | — vasculitis, TTP-HUS, malignant hypertension | Nephrotoxins | — exogenous drugs (e.g., aminoglycosides) or endogenous substances (e.g., myoglobin) | Risk Factors for AKI | 75 years) | Pre-existing conditions: CKD, cardiac failure, peripheral vascular disease, hypertension, hepatic disease, diabetes mellitus | Exposure to nephrotoxic medications

AKI · 4/14 | Aetiology of AKI — Post-Renal & Risk Factors | Post-Renal (5%) | Physical obstruction to the passage of urine | Bladder outlet obstruction | Bilateral kidney obstruction | Unilateral kidney obstruction (in case of solitary kidney) | Why Post-Renal Is Urgent | Obstruction is the most readily reversible cause of AKI | Recovery of renal function is inversely related to the duration of obstruction | Risk Factors for AKI | 75 years) | Pre-existing conditions | — chronic kidney disease (CKD), cardiac failure, peripheral vascular disease, hypertension, hepatic disease, diabetes mellitus | Exposure to nephrotoxic medications | 55% pre-renal, 40% intrinsic, 5% post-renal — the post-renal minority is the most surgically remediable.

AKI · 4/13 | Pre-Renal Azotemia | Mechanism & Hallmark | Transient renal hypoperfusion induces a fall in GFR and produces urinary sodium retention | The hallmark of pre-renal azotemia is its reversibility with treatment of the underlying cause and the lack of structural damage | The 'gold standard' is the response to appropriate fluid repletion — return of renal function to baseline within 24 to 72 hours | Sustained pre-renal azotemia is a primary risk factor for ischemia-induced acute tubular necrosis (ATN) | Common Etiologies | Dehydration | Hypovolemia | Hemodynamic factors compromising renal perfusion: CHF, shock | Treatment | Directed at optimizing volume status with isotonic fluids | In edematous disorders with pre-renal azotemia: treat the underlying disease (heart failure, cirrhosis) | Haemodynamic Monitoring & Support | Fluid choice | — in the absence of hemorrhagic shock, isotonic crystalloids are recommended over colloids (albumin or starches) for initial volume expansion | Blood pressure support | — use vasopressors to maintain perfusion pressure in patients with vasomotor shock at risk for AKI

AKI · 5/13 | Renal AKI — Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) | The type of AKI in the majority of hospitalized patients | Epidemiology & Classification | The type of AKI in hospitalized patients is ATN in the majority of cases | AKI may occur in 2–7% of hospitalized patients in tertiary care centers | The incidence in intensive care units may exceed 25% | Classified by primary site of injury | — tubular (ATN); interstitium (AIN); glomerulus (AGN); vascular | Causes of ATN | 1 — Renal hypoperfusion and renal ischemia: the most common causes | 2 — Nephrotoxic insults: aminoglycosides (10–30% risk); amphotericin B; cisplatin; cyclosporin; temsirolimus | Prevention of Aminoglycoside- & Amphotericin-Related AKI | In patients with normal, steady-state kidney function, aminoglycosides should be administered as a single-dose daily regimen rather than multiple doses | Drug levels for aminoglycosides should be monitored if treatment lasts more than 48 hours | Topical or local applications (respiratory aerosols or antibiotic beads) are preferred over IV application when feasible, to reduce systemic toxicity | Single daily dosing + level monitoring + topical preference = the triad of aminoglycoside nephroprotection.

AKI · 6/13 | Renal AKI — Acute Glomerulonephritis & Interstitial Nephritis | Acute Glomerulonephritis (AGN) | Proteinuria, hematuria and red blood cell (RBC) casts are highly suggestive of glomerulonephritis | Puffiness of the face; blood in urine | Types of glomerular disease | — acute post-infectious GN; lupus nephritis; IgA glomerulonephritis; infective endocarditis; Goodpasture syndrome; Wegener disease (ANCA-associated) | AGN = RBC casts; AIN = WBC casts + eosinophiluria (Hansel stain); ATN = muddy brown casts. | Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN) | Diagnosis suggested by urinalysis: sterile pyuria, white blood cell casts, and eosinophiluria (using Hansel stain) | Most frequently induced by drug therapy | Common causative drugs | — NSAIDs (especially fenoprofen); penicillins and cephalosporins; rifampin; sulfonamides (including furosemide and thiazides); cimetidine, omeprazole, allopurinol; ciprofloxacin and 5-aminosalicylates | Vascular (Renal) AKI | Large vessels | — bilateral renal artery stenosis; bilateral renal vein thrombosis | Small vessels | — vasculitis; malignant hypertension; atherosclerotic or thrombotic emboli; haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS); thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)

AKI · 7/13 | Post-Renal AKI — Obstruction | Etiologies | Upper tract — intrinsic | — nephrolithiasis; blood clot; papillary necrosis; cancer | Upper tract — extrinsic | — retroperitoneal or pelvic malignancy; endometriosis/prolapsed uterus; abdominal aortic or iliac artery aneurysm; retroperitoneal fibrosis | Lower tract | — BPH or prostate cancer; bladder cancer; urethral strictures; bladder stones; blood clots; functional obstruction from neurogenic bladder | Classification of Post-Renal AKI | Level of obstruction: upper tract (ureters) vs lower tract (bladder outlet/urethra) | Degree: partial vs complete | Nature: anatomic (unilateral vs bilateral) or functional | Duration: acute vs chronic | Cause: congenital vs acquired | Why It Matters | Important to rule out quickly: the potential for recovery of renal function is often inversely related to the duration of the obstruction | Clinical Features | Complaints: hematuria, flank/abdominal pain, signs of uremia; oliguria or anuria | Investigation: renal ultrasonography | Ultrasound is the first-line investigation for suspected obstruction — hydronephrosis is the key finding.

AKI · 8/13 | Assessment of a Patient with AKI — Focused History | History of the Cause | Pre-renal clues | — nausea, vomiting, history of dehydration, renal or liver disease | Post-renal clues | — hesitancy, frequency, urgency, weak stream, dribbling, feeling of incomplete bladder emptying, flank pain; history of kidney stones, BPH or spinal cord injury | Any recent illnesses? Fever? Rashes? | Any recent surgery? Cardiovascular instability? | Toxin exposure: new medications (antibiotics, NSAIDs)? IV contrast? | Change in urination, any edema/SOB/weight gain? | History of the AKI Itself | Decreased urine output (urine output can sometimes remain normal) | Fluid retention — edema of legs/ankles/feet; shortness of breath, fatigue, confusion, nausea, weakness | Irregular heartbeat, chest pain/pressure; in severe cases seizures or coma | AKI can be asymptomatic and detected incidentally via lab tests | History of the Complications | Hyperkalaemia, hypo/hypernatraemia, hypercalcaemia | Metabolic acidosis | Pulmonary oedema | Hypertension | Uraemic encephalopathy | Uraemic pericarditis | Symptoms of the Cause — Examples | Dehydration | — thirst, light-headedness, dry mouth, dark urine | Sepsis | — fever, rigors, localized symptoms of the infectious focus | Drug history | — ACE inhibitors (ACEIs), ARBs, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin)

AKI · 9/13 | Volume Assessment & Further Work-up | How to Assess Volume | History — intake, fluid loss, medications | Postural blood pressure and pulse | Daily weights | Fluid balance | Signs of volume depletion | — dry mouth, increased thirst, light-headedness, muscle cramps, extremities cool to the touch, palpitations, reduced and dark urine, syncope | Further Work-up | U/A, urine protein/creatinine, urine eosinophilia | Uric acid | Urine microscopy | — muddy brown casts in ATN; WBC casts in AIN; RBC casts in AGN | 100–150 mL consistent with voiding dysfunction) | Bladder catheterization | Renal ultrasound | Investigations — Urological Perspective | Blood tests | — urea, electrolytes, creatinine, bicarbonate, full blood count (to rule out HUS/TTP if platelets are low), liver function tests (hepatorenal syndrome), Ca²⁺/PO₄³⁻, creatine kinase (CK), blood cultures if sepsis suspected | Urinalysis | — check for blood, protein, leucocytes, or nitrites | Imaging | — ultrasound scan of the renal tract and bladder — within 24 h if obstruction is expected;

AKI · 10/13 | When to Refer to a Nephrologist (Within 24 Hours) | Referral Criteria | A specialist diagnosis is suspected — vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, tubulointerstitial nephritis, or myeloma | AKI has no clear cause | Inadequate response to treatment or associated complications | AKI stage 3 is present | The patient has a renal transplant | Chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 4 or 5 is present | Key Point | Early nephrology input changes outcomes in AKI — referral is mandated within 24 hours of detection when any of the six criteria are met. Urologists contribute by excluding and relieving obstruction, the only truly reversible cause. | Stage 3 AKI, transplant patients, unexplained AKI, suspected specialist diagnoses and inadequate response all mandate referral.

AKI · 11/14 | Management of AKI — Principles & Initial Steps | General Principle | No therapy to date has shown efficacy in treating AKI | Identify the etiology and treat the underlying cause | Optimization of hemodynamics to increase renal perfusion | Initial Management Steps | Stop/avoid nephrotoxic drugs (adjust dosages if necessary) | Fluid resuscitation | Monitor fluid balance (input/output chart, daily weights) | Assess urinary osmolality and sodium | Urethral catheterisation (relieve bladder obstruction, monitor urine output) | Renal ultrasound (consider if post-renal obstruction is suspected) | Treat the underlying cause | Treat complications

AKI · 12/14 | Management of AKI — Treat the Cause & Complications | Treat the Cause | Infections | — administer antibiotics at renal doses | Intrinsic renal disease | — review and adjust medications | Obstruction | — consider catheters, calculus removal, nephrostomies, or surgery | Obstruction is the urologist's domain — relieve it before renal recovery is lost. | Treat Complications | Correct fluid imbalances: strict I/O's, daily weights, determine fluid balance goals daily, fluid selection or diuresis, readjust for urine output recovery, post-diuresis or dialysis | Electrolyte imbalances (low potassium/phosphorus diet) | Metabolic acidosis | Nutrition: adjust protein intake | Medication dosing: adjust for eGFR to avoid under- or overdosing; timing for dialytic therapy; reassess dosing for renal recovery or dialysis modality | Procedural considerations: prefer non-contrast CT, appropriate delay of contrast exposure, prophylaxis

CKD · 3/4 | CKD — Uremia, Manifestations & Screening | Pathophysiology of Uremia | Uremia: a constellation of symptoms in advanced renal failure from three main factors: | 1 — Accumulation of toxins normally excreted by the kidneys | 2 — Loss of renal function (fluid/electrolyte homeostasis and hormonal regulation) | 3 — Progressive systemic inflammation with nutritional and vascular consequences | Clinical Manifestations | Most patients with early-stage (1 & 2) CKD are asymptomatic — CKD is a 'silent killer' | Late-stage CKD: easy fatigability, anorexia, vomiting, cognitive deficits, hiccups, peripheral edema, muscle cramps | Screening | Screening should be performed for all individuals during routine health encounters | Targeted evaluation for those at increased risk: DM, hypertension, CVD, or family history | Screening involves urinary exams for protein/albumin and creatinine assessment

CKD · 4/4 | CKD — Evaluation | History | Underlying causes: hypertension, diabetes, abnormal U/A, pregnancy problems, drug use, family history, autoimmune diseases | Assess for uremic symptoms | Physical Examination | Hypertension and target organ damage | Volume status and edema | Sensory polyneuropathy | Asterixis (flapping tremor) | Pericardial friction rub | Laboratory | Serial serum creatinine, GFR calculation | Serum and urine protein electrophoresis, 24-hour urine protein | Viral markers (HIV, Hep B/C) | Autoimmune markers (ANA, anti-dsDNA) | Serum electrolytes: calcium, phosphorus, vitamin D, PTH | Renal biopsy only if indicated; abdominal U/S is standard imaging | Establishing the Diagnosis & Acute-on-Chronic | Distinguish CKD from acute/subacute kidney disease using historical creatinine records, metabolic bone disease, small kidneys and anemia | Rule out acute-on-chronic | — triggers include ECFV depletion, UTI, urinary obstruction, nephrotoxin exposure, and reactivation/flare of underlying primary disease (e.g., lupus, vasculitis)

CKD · 5/4 | CKD — Management & Slowing Progression | Management Steps | 1 — Establish and treat the underlying cause if possible | 2 — Identify and manage unexpected acute deterioration (reversible causes: decreased renal perfusion — fluid loss, AMI, sepsis, ACEIs; nephrotoxic drugs — aminoglycosides, contrast, NSAIDs; urinary tract obstruction) | 3 — Slow the rate of progression (major factors: intraglomerular hypertension, glomerular hypertrophy; contributing: hyperlipidemia, metabolic acidosis, tubulointerstitial disease) | 4 — Treat metabolic and systemic complications | 5 — Prepare for renal replacement therapy (RRT) | Measures to Slow Progression | Strict control of hypertension | Reduction and control of proteinuria | Tight control of blood sugar (especially diabetics) | Dietary protein restriction | Statin therapy for lipids | Antiplatelet therapy | Smoking cessation

CKD · 6/4 | CKD — Control of Hypertension & Proteinuria | NICE 2014 targets | Blood Pressure Targets | CKD alone: | CKD with diabetes mellitus: | CKD with proteinuria: | Glycemic Control & Diet | Glycemic control: preprandial glucose 90–130 mg/dL; HbA1c | Dietary protein restriction: 0.6–0.8 g/kg/day (KDOQI: 0.60–0.75 g/kg/day); risk of protein-energy malnutrition in advanced CKD | Proteinuria Goals & Drugs of Choice | Proteinuria goal: | Drugs of choice | — ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line for proteinuria (DM, glomerular diseases); combination ACE + ARB is not recommended; second-line: non-dihydropyridine CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil); other antihypertensives if no proteinuria; salt restriction for proteinuria | ACEi/ARB remain the cornerstone of renoprotection — but never combine them.

CKD · 4/3 | CKD — Complications, Anemia & Renal Replacement Therapy | Complications | Of renal dysfunction | — volume overload, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperphosphatemia, renal osteodystrophy, hypertension, anemia, dyslipidemia, sexual dysfunction | Of ESRD | — malnutrition, uremic bleeding, pericarditis, uremic neuropathy, thyroid dysfunction, increased risk of infection (managed via vaccination) | Anemia in CKD | Causes | — relative erythropoietin (EPO) deficiency; diminished RBC survival; bleeding diathesis and iron deficiency; secondary hyperparathyroidism (bone marrow fibrosis); chronic inflammation; hemoglobinopathies; vitamin deficiencies (folate, B12); comorbidities (thyroid dysfunction, pregnancy, HIV, autoimmune disease) | Treatment | — maintain hemoglobin 10.5–12 g/dL; options — RBC transfusions, androgens, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESA); initiate ESA when Hb | Renal Replacement Therapy (RRT) | Early identification of CKD and timely referral to specialists | Clear indications to initiate RRT | — uremic pericarditis and encephalopathy; intractable muscle cramping; persistent anorexia and nausea (not due to other causes such as PUD); evidence of malnutrition; refractory fluid/electrolyte issues (hyperkalemia or ECF volume overload) | CKD complications span every system — anemia management targets Hb 10.5–12 g/dL with ESA + iron.

Transplantation · 2/5 | Renal Transplantation — Introduction, Definitions & ESRD Indications | Introduction & Definitions | Renal transplantation is the preferred treatment for ESRD | Hemodialysis is center-based (2.5–5 hours, 3×/week) | Transplantation offers better quality of life and greater longevity than long-term dialysis | Allograft | — transplant between genetically different individuals of the same species (human to human) | Autograft | — donor and recipient are the same person | Xenograft | — donor and recipient of different species | ESRD — Indications & Risks | Diabetic nephropathy is responsible for 40% of diseases leading to transplantation; diabetic patients are more prone to post-transplant complications | Any patient with GFR | Diseases with significant risk of recurrence in the allograft | — primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS); hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS); membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN); primary oxalosis | Perioperative risk | — patients over age 50 with comorbidities have approximately a 25% risk for complications | Pretransplant infection screening | — HIV, hepatitis B & C, EBV, CMV, syphilis, tuberculosis

Transplantation · 3/5 | Renal Transplantation — Indications for Native Nephrectomy | Indications (Box 47-1) | Symptomatic renal stones not cleared by minimally invasive techniques or lithotripsy | High-grade solid renal tumors with or without acquired renal cystic disease | Polycystic kidneys that are symptomatic, extend below the iliac crest, have been infected, or have solid tumors | Persistent anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody levels | Significant proteinuria not controlled with medical nephrectomy or angioablation | Recurrent pyelonephritis | Grade 4 or 5 vesicoureteral reflux with urinary tract infections | Timing | Ideally nephrectomy ≥ 6 weeks before transplant if a living donor is available | Native nephrectomy removes the sources of infection, bleeding, proteinuria and malignancy that would threaten the allograft.

Transplantation · 2/4 | Renal Transplantation — Allocation & Preservation | Allocation | ABO blood groups | — ABO-incompatible transplantation triggers antibody binding to non-inherited antigens on endothelial cells → complement activation → coagulation → thrombosis → rapid graft loss; achievable if antibody titers are low and antibody production is limited with immunosuppression | MHC/HLA | — the human major histocompatibility complex consists of over 200 genes on chromosome 6p21.3, coding cell surface proteins expressed on renal allografts; recipient leukocytes recognize these proteins and trigger an immune response | Kidney Preservation & Donation | The renal tubular sodium-potassium pump maintains high intracellular potassium; preservation solutions maintain organ viability during transport | UW solution contents | — K⁺ lactobionate 100 mM, KH₂PO₄ 25 mM, MgSO₄ 5 mM, raffinose 30 mM, adenosine 5 mM, glutathione 3 mM, insulin 100 U/L, dexamethasone 8 mg/L, allopurinol 1 mM, hydroxyethyl starch 50 g/L, penicillin 200,000 U/L; pH 7.45, osmolarity 320 ± 5 mOsm/L | Absolute contraindications to donation | 75 is a relative contraindication | Living donor operation | — laparoscopic donor nephrectomy (LDN) is the standard of care — 6% minor complications,

Transplantation · 3/4 | Renal Transplantation — The Surgical Procedure | Wet Ischemia & Positioning | Wet ischemia time (circulatory cessation to organ removal and cold storage) must not exceed 30 minutes | The transplanted kidney is placed in the right or left lower quadrant of the abdomen in an extraperitoneal position; post-transplant the organ is typically easily palpable | Anastomoses | The transplant renal artery is anastomosed to the internal or external iliac artery | The renal vein is anastomosed to the internal or external iliac vein | The transplant ureter is connected to the bladder | Number of Kidneys & Donor Operation | Typically only a single kidney is transplanted | Exception: small pediatric or older cadaveric donor kidneys — both kidneys transplanted into one recipient to ensure adequate renal mass | Living donor: laparoscopic donor nephrectomy (LDN) is the current standard of care — low complication rate (6% minor, | Surgeons must ensure adequate length of the renal vessels and ureter for the recipient's operation | Most LDNs are performed on the left side because the left renal vein is longer; right-sided LDN when necessary to preserve the 'better' kidney for the donor | Extraperitoneal placement in the lower quadrant makes the graft palpable and accessible.

Transplantation · 4/4 | Renal Transplantation — Function, Prognosis & Morbidity | Function & Prognosis | Living donor transplants usually function immediately after surgery | Delayed graft function: ~30% of cadaveric transplants — due to prolonged ischemic cold preservation; continued dialysis until the graft begins to function | Graft survival | — living donor 95% at 1 year, 76% at 5 years; cadaveric 89% at 1 year, 61% at 5 years | Patient survival | — living donor 98% at 1 year, 91% at 5 years; cadaveric 95% at 1 year, 81% at 5 years | Morbidity & Mortality | Infection: most common cause of morbidity and mortality in the first year | Hypertension: 75–85% of recipients; hyperlipidaemia: 60% | Cardiovascular disease: 15.8–23%; diabetes mellitus: 16.9–19.9% (new-onset DM associated with corticosteroid use)

Transplantation · 5/5 | Renal Transplantation — Immunosuppression & Surgical Complications 1–3 | Immunosuppressive Therapy | Renal transplant patients require lifelong immunosuppression to prevent rejection | 'Triple' therapy regimens | — cyclosporine-microemulsion or tacrolimus + mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine + corticosteroids | Sirolimus (available 1994) is now part of standard protocols | Treatment of rejection | — IV corticosteroids — methylprednisolone 250–1000 mg daily or dexamethasone 100 mg daily, for 3 days | Complications 1–3 | Acute vascular occlusion | — 0.5–8% in the first post-transplant week; oligoanuria, ARF; renal vein thrombosis — graft tenderness, dark hematuria, decreased urine; diagnosis: Doppler U/S or radioisotope scan; treatment: surgery | Peritransplant haematoma | — 2–3%, early post-op or related to anticoagulation; severe pain over allograft, decreased Hb/hematocrit, increased creatinine, recurrent hyperkalemia (RBC lysis); diagnosis: CT; treatment: surgery (often allograft nephrectomy) | Urinary leak | — 2–5% during the first month; urine extravasation, ARF, fever, pain, distended abdomen; diagnosis: U/S or radioisotope scan; treatment: Foley catheter and surgery

Transplantation · 6/5 | Renal Transplantation — Surgical Complications 4–6 | Complications 4–6 | Lymphocoele | — 5–15% within the first 3 months (lymph leaking from severed lymphatics); large collections — pain, ARF, frequency, ipsilateral lower extremity edema; can cause iliac vein thrombosis or PE; diagnosis: U/S; treatment: percutaneous drainage | Obstructive uropathy | — 3–6% early post-transplant; extrinsic ureteral compression by lymphocoele or technical issues at the ureteric anastomosis; diagnosis: U/S (hydronephrosis); management: surgical | Renal artery stenosis | — presents late; uncontrolled hypertension, allograft dysfunction, peripheral edema; diagnosis: U/S or MRA | Complication Pattern — Summary | First week | — acute vascular occlusion (0.5–8%) — oligoanuria, ARF; renal vein thrombosis — graft tenderness, dark hematuria | Early post-op / anticoagulation | — peritransplant haematoma (2–3%) — pain, falling Hb, rising creatinine, hyperkalemia | First month | — urinary leak (2–5%) — extravasation, ARF, fever | First 3 months | — lymphocoele (5–15%) — pain, ARF, frequency, ipsilateral edema | Early transplant | — obstructive uropathy (3–6%) — hydronephrosis on U/S | Late | — renal artery stenosis — hypertension, allograft dysfunction, edema | Vascular → haematoma → leak → lymphocoele → obstruction → stenosis: the six surgical complications in order of incidence.

Transplantation · 6/4 | Transplant — Fever & Malignancy | Fever in the Transplant Patient | Infections in the 1st month | — usually standard post-op complications — pneumonia, wound infection, line sepsis, catheter-associated UTI; common pathogens: E. coli (UTI), S. aureus and S. viridans (line sepsis/wound), S. pneumoniae (pneumonia) | Non-infectious causes | — pulmonary atelectasis (early post-op), severe acute rejection, systemic reaction to antilymphocyte antibodies, post-transplant lymphoma (PTLD) | Initial work-up | — FBC with differential, serum creatinine, urine dipstick/analysis; blood and urine cultures; CXR and transplant-specific U/S; additional tests guided by the clinical setting | Malignancy | Significantly higher cancer risk due to: (1) chronic immunosuppression; (2) chronic antigenic stimulation; (3) increased susceptibility to oncogenic viruses; (4) direct neoplastic action of immunosuppressants | 2–5-fold higher risk for cancers of the colon, larynx, lung and bladder (both sexes), and prostate and testicular cancers (men)

Transplantation · 7/4 | Transplant — Pulmonary Complications & Benefits | Pulmonary Complications | Pneumonia is the most common pulmonary complication | Non-opportunistic post-op pneumonia occurs in the 1st month; opportunistic infections predominate thereafter; after the 1st year community-acquired infections are common | Drug interaction | — if macrolides (erythromycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin) are used, doses of cyclosporine, tacrolimus and sirolimus must be reduced | Fever Recap — Non-Infectious & Infectious | Infectious (1st month) | — pneumonia, wound infection, line sepsis, catheter-associated UTI; pathogens: E. coli (UTI), S. aureus and S. viridans (line/wound), S. pneumoniae (pneumonia) | Non-infectious | — pulmonary atelectasis (early post-op), severe acute rejection, reaction to antilymphocyte antibodies, post-transplant lymphoma (PTLD) | Work-up | — FBC with differential, serum creatinine, urine dipstick; blood and urine cultures; CXR and transplant U/S | Benefits of Transplantation | Improved life expectancy | Cardiovascular benefits | Enhanced quality of life — higher life satisfaction, physical and emotional well-being, ability to return to work; uremic complications more fully reversed; fertility often restored | Socioeconomic benefits | $100,000 in the first year but drops to ~ $10,000/year thereafter; mean cumulative costs are equal for the first 3–4 years; transplantation becomes significantly more cost-effective long term | Transplantation is cost-effective long term despite higher first-year costs.

BASICS & RENAL | Basics & Renal — Key Takeaways | Anatomy: kidneys T12–L3 (hilum L1, right lower), 150 g, ~1 million nephrons; hilum — vein anterior, artery, pelvis posterior; Gerota fascia; renal artery divides into 5 non-communicating segments; bladder — oblique intramural ureter = anti-reflux mechanism; prostate 20 g (Lowsley 5 lobes / McNeal zones); urethra 4 cm female / 15 cm male; spermatic cord contents and pampiniform plexus (left → left renal vein). | Embryology: pronephros → mesonephros (Wolffian duct) → metanephros (ureteric bud + metanephrogenic blastema); urorectal septum divides the cloaca; trigone from incorporated mesonephric ducts. | Congenital anomalies: renal agenesis (bilateral lethal, unilateral compatible), adult PKD (AD, 30–50 yrs) vs infantile (AR, lethal at birth), hypoplasia vs dysplasia, malrotation, ectopia (pelvic/iliac/abdominal/thoracic/crossed), horseshoe kidney; ureterocele (cobra head), UPJO (stenosis/aberrant vessels/aganglionic), bladder exstrophy, posterior urethral valves, hypospadias (never circumcise; repair 6–18 months), cryptorchidism (treat before 1 year; laparoscopy for non-palpable; Fowler–Stephens). | Investigations: first morning urine avoids orthostatic proteinuria; microscopy — RBC | 0.75, density ≥ 0.15; KUB, IVU phases (scout → nephrogram → urogram → prone → full bladder → post-micturition), VCUG (reflux, PUV keyhole sign), ascending urethrogram. | AKI: creatinine ↑ ≥ 0.3 mg/dL in 48 h or 1.5× baseline in 7 days, urine | 7, pH | 150. | CKD: damage or GFR | 3 months; KDIGO G1–G5; diabetes 38% of ESRD; ACEi/ARB first-line for proteinuria (NICE: | Transplantation: preferred for ESRD; ABO/HLA compatibility; UW solution; wet ischemia | Anatomy explains embryology, anomalies explain disease, and investigations bridge the two — the foundation of all urology.
