01 | Overview & Renal Injuries | About 10% of all emergency-room injuries involve the genitourinary system. Early diagnosis is essential to prevent serious complications — from initial resuscitation to the surgical treatment of renal trauma. | UROLOGICAL TRAUMA · SECTION 01

Urological Trauma · 1/27 | Introduction & Initial Management | Introduction | About 10% of all injuries seen in the emergency room involve the genitourinary system | Early diagnosis is essential to prevent serious complications | Management Principles | Control of haemorrhage and shock along with resuscitation | Intravenous lines | Urethral catheter in seriously injured patients | In men, before the catheter is inserted, the urethral meatus should be examined carefully for the presence of blood | History | Detailed description of the accident | In gunshot wounds: the type and calibre of the weapon — high-velocity projectiles cause much more extensive damage | Examination | The abdomen and genitalia should be examined for contusions or subcutaneous hematomas, which might indicate deeper injuries to the retroperitoneum and pelvic structures | Fractures of the lower ribs are often associated with renal injuries; pelvic fractures often accompany bladder and urethral injuries | Diffuse abdominal tenderness is consistent with perforated bowel, free intraperitoneal blood or urine, or retroperitoneal hematoma | Patients without life-threatening injuries and with stable blood pressure can undergo more radiographic studies — providing more definitive staging

Urological Trauma · 2/27 | Renal Injuries — Overview & Etiology | Overview | Renal injuries are the most common injuries of the urinary system | Most injuries occur from automobile accidents or sporting mishaps, chiefly in men and boys | Kidneys with existing pathologic conditions (hydronephrosis or malignant tumors) are more readily ruptured from mild trauma | Etiology | Blunt trauma directly to the abdomen, flank, or back is the most common mechanism — 80–85% of all renal injuries | Motor vehicle accidents, fights, falls and contact sports | Vehicle collisions at high speed may result in major renal trauma from rapid deceleration and cause major vascular injury | Gunshot and knife wounds — any such wound in the flank area should be regarded as a cause of renal injury until proved otherwise | Associated abdominal visceral injuries are present in 80% of renal penetrating wounds | Blunt trauma dominates (80–85%); penetrating wounds carry an 80% rate of associated visceral injury.

Urological Trauma · 3/27 | Renal Injuries — Pathology & Classification | Early Pathologic Findings | Lacerations from blunt trauma usually occur in the transverse plane of the kidney — force is transmitted from the center of the impact to the renal parenchyma | In rapid deceleration injuries, the kidney moves upward or downward, causing sudden stretch on the renal pedicle and sometimes complete or partial avulsion | Acute thrombosis of the renal artery may be caused by an intimal tear from rapid deceleration injuries owing to the sudden stretch | Pathologic Classification (Grades 1–5) | Grade 1 (most common) | — renal contusion or bruising of the parenchyma; microscopic hematuria is common, gross hematuria can occur rarely | Grade 2 | — parenchymal laceration into the renal cortex; perirenal hematoma is usually small | Grade 3 | — laceration extending through the cortex into the medulla; bleeding can be significant with a large retroperitoneal hematoma | Grade 4 | — laceration extending into the collecting system; main renal artery thrombosis from blunt trauma, segmental renal vein, or both; or artery injury with contained bleeding | Grade 5 | — multiple Grade 4 parenchymal lacerations, renal pedicle avulsion, or both; main renal vein or artery injury from penetrating trauma

Urological Trauma · 4/27 | Renal Injuries — Clinical Findings & Imaging Indications | Clinical Findings | Microscopic or gross hematuria following trauma to the abdomen indicates injury to the urinary tract | Stab or gunshot wounds to the flank area should alert the physician to possible renal injury whether or not hematuria is present | Some cases of renal vascular injury are not associated with hematuria — almost always due to rapid deceleration accidents, and an indication for imaging | The degree of renal injury does not correspond to the degree of hematuria — gross hematuria may occur in minor trauma and only mild hematuria in major trauma | Symptoms & Signs | Symptoms | — usually visible evidence of abdominal trauma; pain localized to one flank or over the abdomen; associated injuries (ruptured viscera, pelvic fractures) may obscure the renal injury; catheterization usually reveals haematuria; retroperitoneal bleeding may cause abdominal distention, ileus, nausea and vomiting | Signs | — shock or signs of large blood loss from heavy retroperitoneal bleeding; ecchymosis in the flank or upper quadrants; lower rib fractures; diffuse abdominal tenderness — an 'acute abdomen' usually indicates free blood in the peritoneal cavity; a palpable mass may represent a large retroperitoneal hematoma or urinary extravasation | Laboratory Findings | Microscopic or gross haematuria is usually present | The haematocrit may be normal initially, but a drop may be found on serial studies — representing persistent retroperitoneal bleeding and development of a large retroperitoneal hematoma | Hematuria ≠ severity: minor trauma can cause gross hematuria and major vascular injury may cause none.

Urological Trauma · 5/27 | Renal Injuries — Staging & X-Ray Findings | Staging Begins with CT | The most direct and effective means of staging renal injuries | Clearly defines: parenchymal lacerations; urinary extravasation; the extent of the retroperitoneal hematoma; nonviable tissue; injuries to surrounding organs (pancreas, spleen, liver, bowel) | If CT is not available, intravenous pyelogram can be obtained | Causes of Non-Visualization on Excretory Urogram | Total pedicle avulsion | Arterial thrombosis | Severe contusion causing vascular spasm | Absence of the kidney (congenital or from operation) | Arteriography & Radionuclide Scans | Arteriography defines major arterial and parenchymal injuries when previous studies have not fully done so | Arterial thrombosis and avulsion of the renal pedicle are best diagnosed by arteriography — likely when the kidney is not visualized on imaging studies | Radionuclide renal scans have been used in staging renal trauma; in emergency management this technique is less sensitive than arteriography or CT | Non-visualized kidney on urography = pedicle avulsion, thrombosis, severe spasm, or absent kidney.

Urological Trauma · 6/27 | Renal Injuries — Differential Diagnosis & Complications | Differential Diagnosis | Trauma to the abdomen and flank areas is not always associated with renal injury | In such cases: no hematuria, and the results of imaging studies are normal | Early Complications | Haemorrhage is the most important immediate complication of renal injury | Heavy retroperitoneal bleeding may result in rapid collapse | Patients must be observed closely, with careful monitoring of blood pressure and hematocrit | Late Complications | Hypertension | Hydronephrosis | Arteriovenous fistula | Calculus formation | Pyelonephritis | Renal atrophy may occur from vascular compromise — detected by follow-up urography | Follow-Up | Careful monitoring of blood pressure for several months to watch for hypertension | At 3–6 months: follow-up excretory urogram or CT to be certain that perinephric scarring has not caused hydronephrosis or vascular compromise

Urological Trauma · 7/27 | Renal Injuries — Treatment & Prognosis | Emergency Measures | The objectives of early management: prompt treatment of shock and haemorrhage; complete resuscitation; evaluation of associated injuries | Surgical Measures — Blunt Injuries | Minor renal injuries from blunt trauma account for 85% of cases and do not usually require operation | Bleeding stops spontaneously with bed rest and hydration | Indications for surgery | — persistent retroperitoneal bleeding; urinary extravasation; evidence of nonviable renal parenchyma; renal pedicle injuries — less than 5% of all renal injuries | Aggressive preoperative staging allows complete definition of injury before operation | Penetrating Injuries & Complications | Penetrating injuries should be surgically explored | Rare exception: complete staging showing only minor parenchymal injury with no urinary extravasation | In 80% of penetrating injury cases, associated organ injury requires operation — renal exploration is only an extension of this procedure | Treatment of complications | — retroperitoneal urinoma or perinephric abscess demands prompt surgical drainage; malignant hypertension requires vascular repair or nephrectomy; hydronephrosis may require surgical correction or nephrectomy | Prognosis | With careful follow-up, most renal injuries have an excellent prognosis — spontaneous healing and return of renal function | Follow-up excretory urography and blood pressure monitoring ensure detection and management of late hydronephrosis and hypertension

02 | Ureteric & Bladder Injuries | Ureteral injury is rare but dangerous — usually iatrogenic during pelvic surgery. Bladder rupture accompanies pelvic fractures in 90% of cases, dividing into extraperitoneal and intraperitoneal forms. | UROLOGICAL TRAUMA · SECTION 02

Urological Trauma · 8/27 | Injuries to the Ureter — Introduction & Pathogenesis | Introduction — When Does It Occur? | Ureteral injury is rare | 1 — Difficult pelvic surgical procedure: the ureter may be inadvertently ligated and cut | 2 — Endoscopic basket manipulation of ureteral calculi | 3 — Gunshot wounds | 4 — Rapid deceleration accidents may avulse the ureter from the renal pelvis | Prognosis Depends on Timing | Excellent if the diagnosis is made early and prompt corrective surgery is done | Delay in diagnosis worsens the prognosis because of infection, hydronephrosis, abscess and fistula formation | Pathogenesis — If the Ureter Is Partially Divided | Early | — 1 — urinary extravasation; 2 — ileus and peritonitis; 3 — large urinoma | Late | — 1 — ureterovaginal or ureterocutaneous fistula formation; 2 — reactive fibrosis and stricture; 3 — mild to moderate hydronephrosis | Partial division → extravasation early, fistula/stricture/hydronephrosis late.

Urological Trauma · 9/28 | Injuries to the Ureter — Clinical Findings | Clinical Findings | Unilateral complete or partial ligation | — fever, flank pain and lower quadrant pain, paralytic ileus; ureterovaginal or cutaneous fistula within the first 10 postoperative days | Bilateral complete ligation | — anuria | Sustained stab or gunshot wounds to the retroperitoneum | — ureteral injuries should be suspected; the mid portion of the ureter is the most common site of penetrating injury; usually associated vascular and other abdominal visceral injuries | Signs | Signs of acute peritonitis | Urine leakage: watery discharge from the wound or vagina may be identified as urine by determining the creatinine concentration | Intravenous injection of 10 mL of indigo carmine will appear in the urine as dark blue | Laboratory Findings | Ureteral injury from external violence is manifested by microscopic hematuria in 90% of cases | Urine analysis and other laboratory studies are of little use in diagnosis when injury has occurred from other causes

Urological Trauma · 10/28 | Injuries to the Ureter — Imaging Findings | Imaging Findings | KUB | — a plain film may demonstrate a large area of increased density in the pelvis or retroperitoneum | IVU | — delayed excretion with hydronephrosis; partial transection — more rapid excretion, persistent hydronephrosis and contrast extravasation at the site of injury on delayed films | CTU & 3D reconstruction | — delineate the injury precisely | Ultrasonography | — outlines hydroureter or urinary extravasation developing into a urinoma — perhaps the best means of ruling out ureteral injury in the early postoperative period | Radionuclide scanning | — demonstrates delayed excretion on the injured side; great benefit in assessing renal function after surgical correction | Diagnosis Summary | IVU: delayed excretion + hydronephrosis; extravasation at the site of injury on delayed films | US: best early postoperative screening tool — urinoma formation | Radionuclide scan: delayed excretion + function assessment after correction | Ultrasound is the best early means of ruling out ureteral injury in the postoperative period.

Urological Trauma · 10/27 | Injuries to the Ureter — Diagnosis, Complications & Treatment | Differential Diagnosis | Postoperative bowel obstruction | Deep wound infection | Acute pyelonephritis — sonography shows normal results, and urography shows no evidence of obstruction | Complications | Stricture formation with resulting hydronephrosis | Chronic urinary extravasation leads to urinoma formation | Pyelonephritis from hydronephrosis and urinary infection | Treatment | Immediate re-exploration in the operating room when the injury occurs | Delayed repair | — within 7 to 10 days if no infection, abscess or other complications exist | Percutaneous nephrostomy | — if the injury is recognized late, or if the patient has significant complications | Goals of exploration | — complete debridement; tension-free spatulated anastomosis; watertight closure; ureteral stenting; retroperitoneal drainage | Repair principles: debride, spatulate, anastomose without tension, stent, drain.

Urological Trauma · 11/27 | Injuries to the Urinary Bladder — Introduction & Pathogenesis | Introduction | About 15% of all pelvic fractures are associated with concomitant bladder or urethral injuries | Pelvic fracture accompanies bladder rupture in 90% of cases | Iatrogenic injury may result from gynaecologic and other extensive pelvic procedures, hernia repairs and transurethral operations | Pathogenesis & Pathology | Fragments from the fracture site may perforate the bladder, resulting in extraperitoneal rupture | When the bladder is filled to near full capacity, a direct blow to the lower abdomen may result in intraperitoneal rupture | If the diagnosis is not established immediately and the urine is sterile, no symptoms may be noted for several days | If the urine is infected: immediate peritonitis and acute abdomen; deep pelvic abscess and severe pelvic inflammation develop | Two Rupture Patterns | Extraperitoneal rupture | — caused by bone fragments perforating the bladder — the commoner pattern | Intraperitoneal rupture | — from a direct blow on a full bladder — urine enters the peritoneal cavity | Sterile urine → delayed symptoms; infected urine → immediate peritonitis | Fracture fragments → extraperitoneal; full-bladder blow → intraperitoneal.

Urological Trauma · 12/27 | Injuries to the Urinary Bladder — Clinical Findings | Clinical Findings | The diagnosis of pelvic fracture can be made initially in the ER by lateral compression on the bony pelvis — the fracture site will show crepitus and be painful to the touch | Symptoms | — usually a history of lower abdominal trauma; patients are unable to urinate, but when spontaneous voiding occurs, gross haematuria is usually present; pelvic or lower abdominal pain | Signs | — heavy bleeding associated with pelvic fracture may result in hemorrhagic shock, usually from venous disruption of pelvic vessels; evidence of external injury from a gunshot or stab wound in the lower abdomen; an acute abdomen may occur with intraperitoneal rupture; on rectal examination, landmarks may be indistinct because of a large pelvic hematoma | Laboratory Findings — Catheterization Rules | Catheterization usually is required in patients with pelvic trauma — but NOT if bloody urethral discharge is noted | Bloody urethral discharge indicates urethral injury — a urethrogram is necessary before catheterization | When catheterization is done, gross or (less commonly) microscopic haematuria is usually present | Urine taken from the bladder at the initial catheterization should be cultured to determine whether infection is present | Imaging Findings | A plain abdominal film demonstrates pelvic fractures | A CT scan should be obtained to establish whether kidney and ureteral injuries are present

Urological Trauma · 13/27 | Injuries to the Urinary Bladder — Ascending Cystogram | Ascending Cystogram Technique | 1 — The bladder should be filled with 300 mL of contrast material | 2 — Contrast medium should be allowed to drain out completely, and a second film of the abdomen should be obtained | 3 — It demonstrates areas of extraperitoneal extravasation of blood and urine that may not appear on the filling film | 4 — With intraperitoneal extravasation, free contrast medium is visualized in the abdomen | Complications | A pelvic abscess may develop from extraperitoneal bladder rupture; if the urine becomes infected, the pelvic hematoma becomes infected too | Intraperitoneal bladder rupture with extravasation of urine into the abdominal cavity causes delayed peritonitis | Partial incontinence may result from bladder injury when the laceration extends into the bladder neck | The post-drainage film is essential — extraperitoneal extravasation may only appear after the bladder empties.

Urological Trauma · 14/28 | Injuries to the Urinary Bladder — Treatment | Surgical Measures | Shock and haemorrhage should be treated | A lower midline abdominal incision is used | Pelvic hematoma, which is usually lateral, should be avoided — entering it can result in increased bleeding from release of tamponade and in infection of the hematoma, with subsequent pelvic abscess | The bladder should be opened in the midline and carefully inspected | After repair, a suprapubic cystostomy tube is usually left in place to ensure complete urinary drainage and control of bleeding | Extraperitoneal Rupture | Can be successfully managed with urethral catheter drainage only — typically, 10 days will provide adequate healing time | Large blood clots in the bladder or injuries involving the bladder neck should be managed surgically | The bladder is opened in the midline, carefully inspected, and lacerations closed from within

Urological Trauma · 15/28 | Bladder Rupture — Intraperitoneal Repair & Prognosis | Intraperitoneal Rupture | Repaired via a transperitoneal approach after careful transvesical inspection and closure of any other perforations | The peritoneum must be closed carefully over the area of injury | The bladder is then closed in separate layers by absorbable suture | All extravasated fluid from the peritoneal cavity should be removed before closure | Prognosis | With appropriate treatment, the prognosis is excellent | The suprapubic cystostomy tube can be removed within 10 days, and the patient can usually void normally | Patients with lacerations extending into the bladder neck area may be temporarily incontinent, but full control is usually regained | Transperitoneal approach → close peritoneum → close bladder in layers → evacuate all extravasated fluid.

03 | Urethral Injuries | Posterior urethral injuries ride with pelvic fractures; anterior urethral injuries follow straddle falls. Blood at the meatus is the single most important sign — classification and staged reconstruction determine the outcome. | UROLOGICAL TRAUMA · SECTION 03

Urological Trauma · 15/27 | Injuries to the Urethra — Introduction | Anatomic Divisions | Posterior urethra | — consisting of the prostatic and membranous portions | Anterior urethra | — consisting of the bulbous and pendulous portions | Epidemiology | Urethral injuries are uncommon and occur most often in men | Usually associated with pelvic fractures or straddle-type falls | Various parts of the urethra may be lacerated, transected, or contused | Key Point | Posterior urethra = prostatic + membranous portions. Anterior urethra = bulbous + pendulous portions. Pelvic fractures injure the posterior urethra; straddle falls injure the anterior (bulbous) urethra. | Blood at the urethral meatus is the single most important sign of urethral injury.

Urological Trauma · 16/27 | Injuries to the Posterior Urethra — Clinical Findings | Introduction & Mechanism | The membranous urethra passes through the pelvic floor and voluntary urinary sphincter — the portion of the posterior urethra most likely to be injured | When pelvic fractures occur from blunt trauma, the membranous urethra is sheared from the prostatic apex at the prostate-membranous junction | Symptoms & Signs | Symptoms | — lower abdominal pain and inability to urinate; a history of crushing injury to the pelvis is usually obtained | Blood at the meatus | — the single most important sign of urethral injury | Catheter hazard | — an attempt to pass a urethral catheter may result in infection of the periprostatic and perivesical hematoma and conversion of an incomplete laceration to a complete one | Other signs | — suprapubic tenderness; pelvic fracture; a large pelvic hematoma may be palpated; rectal examination may reveal a large hematoma with the prostate displaced superiorly — but a tense pelvic hematoma may resemble the prostate on palpation; perineal or suprapubic contusions | Prostatic Displacement — The Caveat | Superior displacement of the prostate does not occur if the puboprostatic ligaments remain intact | Partial disruption of the membranous urethra (currently 10% of cases) is not accompanied by prostatic displacement | Never pass a catheter when blood is present at the meatus — image first.

Urological Trauma · 17/27 | Injuries to the Posterior Urethra — Imaging & Classification | Imaging Findings | Ascending urethrogram (using 20 to 30 mL of water-soluble contrast material) shows the site of extravasation at the prostate-membranous junction | Ordinarily, there is free extravasation of contrast material into the perivesical space | Incomplete prostate-membranous disruption is seen as minor extravasation, with a portion of contrast material passing into the prostatic urethra and bladder | Classification of Urethral Injuries | Type I | — intact but stretched posterior urethra following blunt trauma | Type II | — posterior urethral rupture above the intact urogenital diaphragm following blunt trauma | Type III | — posterior urethral rupture extending through the urogenital diaphragm to involve the bulbous urethra following blunt trauma | Type IV | — bladder neck injury | Instrumental Examination | The only instrumentation involved should be for urethrography | Catheterization or urethroscopy should not be done — these procedures pose an increased risk of hematoma, infection and further damage to partial urethral disruptions

Urological Trauma · 18/27 | Injuries to the Posterior Urethra — Differential Diagnosis & Complications | Differential Diagnosis | Bladder rupture may be associated with posterior urethral injuries in approximately 20% of cases | Cystography cannot be done preoperatively, since a urethral catheter should not be passed | Careful evaluation of the bladder at operation is necessary | The Three Complications | Stricture | Impotence | Incontinence | Complication Rates — Primary Repair vs Delayed Reconstruction | Complication | Primary repair & anastomosis | Suprapubic cystostomy + delayed repair | Stricture | about 50% | reduced to about 5% | Impotence | 30–80% (mean ~50%) | reduced to 30–35% | Incontinence | one-third of patients | reduced to less than 5% | Delayed reconstruction after suprapubic drainage dramatically reduces all three complications.

Urological Trauma · 19/27 | Injuries to the Posterior Urethra — Treatment | Emergency & Immediate Management | Shock and haemorrhage should be treated | Urethral catheterization should be avoided | Suprapubic cystostomy | — provides urinary drainage for 3 months; allows resolution of the pelvic hematoma, and the prostate and bladder slowly return to their anatomic positions | Incomplete laceration | — heals spontaneously — the suprapubic cystostomy can be removed within 2 to 3 weeks | The cystostomy tube should not be removed before voiding cystourethrography shows that no extravasation persists | Delayed Urethral Reconstruction | Reconstruction of the urethra after 3 months | Before reconstruction: combined cystogram and urethrogram to determine the exact length of the urethral stricture — usually 1–2 cm long, situated immediately posterior to the pubic bone | The preferred approach: single-stage reconstruction — direct excision of the strictured area and anastomosis of the bulbous urethra directly to the apex of the prostate | A 16F silicone urethral catheter should be left in place along with a suprapubic cystostomy | Catheters are removed within a month, and the patient is then able to void | Immediate Urethral Realignment | Some surgeons prefer to realign the urethra immediately | Persistent bleeding and surrounding hematoma create technical problems | The incidence of stricture, impotence and incontinence appears to be higher than with immediate cystostomy and delayed reconstruction

Urological Trauma · 20/27 | Injuries to the Posterior Urethra — Follow-Up & Prognosis | Treatment of Complications | Approximately 1 month after the delayed reconstruction: remove the urethral catheter and obtain a voiding cystogram through the suprapubic cystostomy tube | If the cystogram shows a patent area of reconstruction free of extravasation, the suprapubic catheter can be removed | If there is extravasation or stricture: maintain the suprapubic cystostomy; obtain a follow-up urethrogram within 2 months to watch for stricture development | Stricture, if present ( | The patient may be impotent for several months after delayed repair; impotence is permanent in about 10% of patients; implantation of a penile prosthesis is indicated if impotence is still present 2 years after reconstruction | Incontinence after posterior urethral rupture and delayed repair is rare ( | Prognosis | If complications can be avoided, the prognosis is excellent | Urinary infections ultimately resolve with appropriate management | Follow the 1-month cystogram rule; short strictures (

Urological Trauma · 21/27 | Injuries to the Anterior Urethra — Introduction & Pathogenesis | Introduction | The anterior urethra is the portion distal to the urogenital diaphragm | Straddle injury may cause laceration or contusion of the urethra | Self-instrumentation or iatrogenic instrumentation may cause partial disruption | Pathogenesis & Pathology | Contusion of the urethra is a sign of crush injury without urethral disruption — perineal hematoma usually resolves without complications | Laceration: a severe straddle injury may result in laceration of part of the urethral wall, allowing extravasation of urine | If the extravasation is unrecognized, it may extend into the scrotum, along the penile shaft, and up to the abdominal wall | It is limited only by Colles' fascia and often results in sepsis, infection and serious morbidity | Extravasation Anatomy | Urine extravasation tracks: scrotum → penile shaft → anterior abdominal wall | Boundary: Colles' fascia | Uncontrolled extravasation → sepsis and serious morbidity | Colles' fascia confines anterior urethral extravasation — the classic 'waterfall scrotum'.

Urological Trauma · 22/27 | Injuries to the Anterior Urethra — Clinical Findings | Symptoms | There is usually a history of a fall, and in some cases a history of instrumentation | Bleeding from the urethra is usually present | There is local pain in the perineum and sometimes a massive perineal hematoma | If voiding has occurred and extravasation is noted, sudden swelling in the area will be present | If diagnosis has been delayed, sepsis and severe infection may be present | Signs | The perineum is very tender, and a mass may be found | Rectal examination reveals a normal prostate | The patient usually has a desire to void, but voiding should not be allowed until assessment of the urethra is complete | No attempt should be made to pass a urethral catheter; if the patient's bladder is overdistended, percutaneous suprapubic cystostomy can be done as a temporary procedure | Laboratory Findings | Blood loss is not usually excessive, particularly if secondary injury has occurred | The white count may be elevated with infection | Do not allow voiding; do not catheterize — a normal prostate on DRE distinguishes anterior from posterior injury.

Urological Trauma · 23/27 | Injuries to the Anterior Urethra — Imaging & Complications | X-Ray Findings | A urethrogram, with instillation of 15–20 mL of water-soluble contrast material, demonstrates extravasation and the location of injury | A contused urethra shows no evidence of extravasation | Complications | Bleeding | — heavy bleeding from corpus spongiosum injury may occur in the perineum as well as through the urethral meatus; pressure applied to the perineum over the site usually controls bleeding; if haemorrhage cannot be controlled, immediate operation is required | Infection and sepsis | — the complications of urinary extravasation are chiefly sepsis and infection; aggressive debridement and drainage are required if there is infection | Stricture | — a common complication, but surgical reconstruction may not be required unless the stricture significantly reduces urinary flow rates | Contusion vs Laceration on Urethrogram | Contusion: crush injury without disruption — no extravasation on urethrogram | Laceration: part of the wall divided — extravasation visible with 15–20 mL contrast | The extent of extravasation dictates conservative vs surgical management | 15–20 mL for the anterior urethra (20–30 mL for the posterior) — less volume, more distal.

Urological Trauma · 24/27 | Injuries to the Anterior Urethra — Treatment & Prognosis | General Measures | Major blood loss usually does not occur from straddle injury | If heavy bleeding does occur: local pressure for control, followed by resuscitation | Urethral Lacerations | Suprapubic cystostomy may be used | If only minor extravasation is noted on the urethrogram: a voiding study can be performed within 7 days after suprapubic catheter drainage | In more extensive injuries: wait 2–3 weeks before doing a voiding study through the suprapubic catheter | Healing at the site may result in stricture formation — most are not severe and do not require surgical reconstruction | The suprapubic cystostomy catheter may be removed if no extravasation is documented | Extensive Extravasation & Immediate Repair | Laceration with extensive urinary extravasation | — after major laceration, extravasation may involve the perineum, scrotum and lower abdomen — drainage of these areas is indicated; suprapubic cystostomy for urinary diversion is required; infection and abscess formation are common and require antibiotic therapy | Immediate repair | — can be performed, but the procedure is difficult and the incidence of associated stricture is high | Prognosis | Urethral stricture is a major complication but in most cases does not require surgical reconstruction | If, when the stricture resolves, urinary flow rates are poor and urinary infection and urethral fistula are present, reconstruction is required
